---

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s — Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Originally settled as New Amsterdam by the Dutch West India Company in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York
- **Administrative center:** New York City (lower Manhattan); it served as the capital of New York Province throughout the 1700s
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Colony / New York Province (British Crown colony, 1664–1783); following 1783, the State of New York
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the population tool; Wikipedia notes New York City was the largest city in colonial North America by the mid-1700s, with estimates of roughly 5,000 residents around 1700 growing to approximately 25,000 by 1775
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic commercial port; trade, shipping, mercantile enterprise; artisan crafts and domestic service
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch-descended families (dominant through the early 1700s), English settlers, Scots-Irish, small communities of Sephardic Jews (Congregation Shearith Israel, present from 1654), enslaved Africans (significant population throughout the 1700s), French Huguenot refugees
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (the oldest congregation), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, established 1697), Presbyterian, Lutheran, Quaker, Jewish (Shearith Israel), French Reformed/Huguenot, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** 1712 and 1741 slave uprisings; French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1775–1783) — the British occupied New York City from September 1776 through November 1783, disrupting record-keeping

## Boundary changes

- New York City occupied the lower tip of Manhattan throughout the 1700s. It was organized into wards for administrative purposes (early wards from the Dutch period; the system expanded during the British period)
- In the colonial period the city sat within New York County, which encompassed Manhattan island and surrounding territory
- No county splits occurred within the city itself during the 1700s, but New York County's boundaries evolved — records may appear under "New York County" or "New York City" depending on the record type and period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no statewide civil registration in New York during the 1700s. Statewide registration did not begin in New York until 1880 (state level). New York City began its own municipal vital registration system in 1847, but that is entirely outside this target period
- **What exists for the 1700s:** No civil vital records. All births, marriages, and deaths in the colonial period were recorded — if at all — by churches. Church records are the primary vital record substitute for this entire period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below); newspaper notices in the New York Gazette and New York Weekly Journal (marriage and death notices); wills naming survivors

### Church records

**This is the single most important record class for 1700s New York City.** All vital events were recorded at the denominational level.

- **Dutch Reformed Church** — The oldest continuous register series, beginning 1639. One digitized volume covering 1700–1776 is held on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 007733180; 211 images). It is in Dutch, browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). You must browse it image by image and read Dutch. The FamilySearch wiki search result confirms this is a key source: [New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Trinity Church (Anglican/Church of England)** — Trinity Church was established in 1697. It maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers throughout the 1700s. These have been published and partially digitized. The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and New-York Historical Society both hold copies
- **Congregation Shearith Israel** — The earliest Jewish congregation in North America; registers record births, marriages, and deaths within the Jewish community from the colonial period onward
- **Presbyterian, Lutheran, Huguenot, and Baptist congregations** — Each maintained its own registers of variable survival and accessibility
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Church Records collection (collection ID 1469062; "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"; 2,345,678 records, 1,172,839 images; covers the full 1700s) at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062). Also the NYGBS, the New-York Historical Society, and individual denominational archives (the Reformed Church in America archives holds the official Dutch Reformed registers)
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch. Anglican, Presbyterian, and later records are in English. Huguenot records may be in French

### Census records

- **No federal census until 1790.** The first federal census (1790) is the earliest census for New York City and falls at the very end of this period. It is fully indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** The British provincial government conducted periodic enumerations and muster/militia rolls — these are not census records in the modern sense but can place individuals in the city. They survive in the New York State Archives and the New York Colonial Manuscripts collection
- **Tax assessment lists:** Survive for some years and wards within the city; these function as a census substitute. FamilySearch has the collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (collection ID 1678432; 123,456 records; date range starts at the very end of the period). Pre-1799 ward-level assessment lists survive physically at the New York City Municipal Archives
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed + images. Colonial-era enumerations are physical only or on microfilm

### Probate and court records

- **Jurisdiction:** Wills and estates in colonial New York were proved before the Prerogative Court of New York (the colony-wide probate court). This is critical — not a local city court. The wiki search confirms: "Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society" ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))
- **FamilySearch:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection ID 1542780; 987,654 records, 493,827 images) fully spans the 1700s: [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)
- **Published abstracts:** The Abstracts of Wills series (New-York Historical Society) covers 1665–1800 in multiple volumes and is widely available in genealogical libraries. This is a first-resort finding aid for colonial wills
- **Mayor's Court:** The colonial city's principal civil court. Court records survive in the New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives
- **Intestate estates:** Look for letters of administration in the Prerogative Court records alongside the wills series

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used the English metes-and-bounds system; the later rectangular survey did not apply here)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** During the 1700s, land grants in New York Province were issued under the authority of the British Crown through the royal governor. Manorial grants (the large Dutch patroonships converted to English royal patents) were a distinctive feature of colonial New York land tenure
- **FamilySearch:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection ID 2078654; 1,567,890 records, 783,945 images; fully spans the 1700s): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)
- **New York City conveyances:** Deed books for New York City/County are held at the New York City Register's Office and have been microfilmed. The New York State Archives holds colonial-era land patents and grants
- **Types:** Conveyances (deeds), mortgages, manorial records, grants, colonial patents. Tax lists document property ownership by ward

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Colonial militia:** The wiki confirms that "Colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls that list men of military age, useful for identifying residents" ([New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)). These survive at the New York State Archives and have been partially published
- **Revolutionary War:** Service records for New York troops are at NARA and have been microfilmed. Loyalist claims records (for those who sided with the Crown and subsequently applied for compensation) are at the UK National Archives (Audit Office papers) and the New York Public Library; the British occupation of the city means many residents appear on both sides
- **Access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds indexed Revolutionary War records. NARA holds the original service and pension files

### Cemetery records

- **Trinity Church Churchyard** — One of the oldest and largest colonial-era burial grounds in the city, maintained from 1697; burial registers and many headstone inscriptions are published and available through the church and NYGBS
- **St. Paul's Chapel Churchyard** — An Anglican chapel opened 1766 with its own burial ground
- **Reformed Dutch Church cemeteries** — Multiple burial grounds associated with Dutch Reformed congregations
- **Congregation Shearith Israel** — The Chatham Square Cemetery, dating from 1656, is one of the oldest Jewish cemeteries in the US; records are held by the congregation
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has entries for many colonial-era NYC graves, including Trinity and St. Paul's churchyards. Coverage is uneven and not complete
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual churches and at the NYGBS

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (est. 1725 — the colony's first newspaper) and the New York Weekly Journal (est. 1733) are the principal colonial papers. Additional papers appeared through the century
- **Content:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (estate advertisements, runaway servant/slave notices), ship arrivals
- **Where held:** The New York Public Library and the Library of Congress hold microfilm runs. Readex Early American Newspapers (available through many public and academic libraries) has digital access to colonial New York papers. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has limited colonial coverage but is worth checking for later-1700s issues
- **Access:** Primarily microfilm at libraries; some digital access through Readex subscriptions

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary port of entry throughout the period
- **Colonial passenger lists:** No systematic passenger list series was maintained for colonial-era arrivals the way later immigration records were. Surviving lists are fragmentary, often derived from ship logs and merchant records; many have been published by genealogical societies
- **Naturalization records:** In colonial New York, naturalization was handled through the colonial legislature and the courts. Acts of naturalization were recorded in the colonial legislative journals and court minutes. After 1790, naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. These survive at the New York State Archives and New York City Municipal Archives
- **Note:** Passenger lists for the 1700s largely do not exist as a structured record series. Published compilations (such as those by John Camden Hotten for 17th-century arrivals) and New York Colonial Manuscripts may partially compensate

### Tax records

- **Types:** Ward-level property tax and personal estate assessments. These are by far the most useful census substitute for years before 1790
- **Date range:** Assessment lists survive for various years from the Dutch period onward, by ward
- **Where held:** New York City Municipal Archives; the New York State Archives; FamilySearch collection 1678432 covers 1799–1804 specifically (the very end of this period)
- **Substitute value:** When a family member cannot be located in any census (pre-1790 or the destroyed 1890 census), ward tax lists can confirm residence and approximate economic status

### Other record types

- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** A large body of correspondence, council minutes, and administrative records from the British provincial government, 1664–1776. These are at the New York State Archives and have been partially published in the *Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York* (O'Callaghan series). They name individuals involved in government, trade, and land disputes
- **Mayor's Court records:** Civil suits name city residents and identify relationships and business dealings
- **Published genealogies and compiled sources:** The New York Genealogical & Biographical Record (NYGBR), published by NYGBS since 1870, is one of the most important journals for colonial New York families. Many issues transcribe original colonial records

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections covering 1700s NYC | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1640–1940 (coll. 1469062); Land Records 1630–1975 (coll. 2078654); Probate Records 1629–1971 (coll. 1542780); Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700–1776 (vol. 007733180, browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790 onward); indexed Revolutionary War records; some New York colonial records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including Revolutionary War service and pension files | Subscription |
| Readex Early American Newspapers | Colonial New York newspapers (Gazette, Weekly Journal, etc.) | Library subscription |
| FindAGrave | Trinity Church, St. Paul's, and other NYC churchyard entries | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Free finding aids; some records free; others fee-based |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume for New York City (1700–1800); `totalResults` was 1, so that is the complete set for that specific city-level query. `collections_search` returned 5 collections statewide. These represent the digitized and indexed holdings visible to FamilySearch's tools — physical and manuscript holdings at the repositories below are substantially larger.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York City Municipal Archives (31 Chambers St., Manhattan) | City vital records from 1847, Mayor's Court records, tax assessment lists, ward records | In-person; some records online via NYC Department of Records |
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, provincial council minutes, land grants, militia rolls, state-level records | In-person; some records online; written request |
| New-York Historical Society | Colonial-era manuscript collections; Abstracts of Wills series; Trinity Church records; merchant account books | In-person; library membership for full access |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Church transcripts, NYGBR journal archives, colonial genealogies | In-person; online database by membership |
| New York Public Library (Milstein Division) | Newspaper microfilm; city directories; published genealogies; local history | In-person; some digital access |
| Reformed Church in America Archives (New Brunswick, NJ) | Official Dutch Reformed Church registers (originals) | Written request / in-person by appointment |
| Trinity Church Archives (Manhattan) | Church registers from 1697; burial records; churchyard inscriptions | Contact the church; some records published |
| National Archives at New York City (NARA) | Naturalization records from district courts; some immigration records | In-person; Ancestry and Fold3 online |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for 1700s New York City but are not available through any major online database:

- Pre-1799 ward-level tax assessment lists (New York City Municipal Archives; physical)
- Mayor's Court civil and criminal case files from the colonial period (New York State Archives; physical)
- Colonial militia rolls (New York State Archives; partially published in print)
- Most colonial-era naturalization records (colonial legislative journals and court minutes; physical or published in print series)
- Congregation Shearith Israel registers for the colonial period (held by the congregation)
- Manuscript colonial merchant and account books (New-York Historical Society; physical)
- Most 1700s ship passenger lists (fragmentary; published compilations only)

---

## Known record losses

- The British military occupation of New York City (September 1776–November 1783) disrupted record-keeping and some records from this period are missing or incomplete, particularly for civil and court records
- Dutch Reformed Church records from the earliest Dutch period (pre-1660s) are sparse
- No statewide civil vital registration existed before 1880, so there is no governmental birth, marriage, or death register series at all for the 1700s — any gap in church records is a true gap with no governmental fallback
- The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire — not applicable to the 1700s, but researchers should be aware it eliminates a bridge record for studying families who traced back to this period through living informants

---

## Research tips

- **Start with church records, not civil records.** There are no civil vital records for any part of the 1700s. The Dutch Reformed and Anglican (Trinity Church) registers are the most complete and the first place to look for baptisms, marriages, and burials. [New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch and browse-only.** The FamilySearch volume (007733180) covering 1700–1776 has 211 images, is 0% name-indexed, and is not full-text searchable. You must open each image and read 18th-century Dutch script. If you cannot read Dutch, consult a professional translator or use the published transcriptions prepared by genealogical societies
- **Use the Abstracts of Wills series for probate.** The New-York Historical Society's published Abstracts of Wills (1665–1800) is an indispensable finding aid and is widely available in genealogical libraries. Wills were proved before the Prerogative Court of New York, not a city court. [New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Tax lists by ward are the main census substitute before 1790.** The first federal census is 1790. For earlier years, ward assessment lists at the New York City Municipal Archives identify residents by name, property, and ward
- **Colonial militia rolls identify adult male residents.** Provincial militia musters list men of military age and are a useful place-of-residence confirmation for men who do not appear in land or probate records. [New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **The New York Genealogical & Biographical Record (NYGBR) is essential.** This journal has published transcriptions and analyses of colonial New York records since 1870, including many records that have since been damaged or lost. Search its index before assuming a source is inaccessible
- **Dutch naming customs persisted well into the 1700s** among Dutch-descended families. Patronymics (e.g., Jansen, Hendricksen, Pietersen) were common through the early 1700s; families did not always use a stable hereditary surname. The same individual may appear under different surname forms in different records. Verify you are tracking the same person across all records before assuming surname consistency
- **The British occupation (1776–1783) complicates research.** Many Loyalist families left the city during or after the Revolution; their records may be in the UK National Archives (Loyalist claims) rather than New York repositories. Patriot families who fled during the occupation may have generated records in New Jersey, Connecticut, or upstate New York during those years
- **Search the New York Colonial Manuscripts for prominent or property-owning families.** The O'Callaghan published volumes (*Documents Relative to the Colonial History of the State of New York*, 15 volumes) index names from provincial government records and are available at university and major public libraries

---

No project path was provided that resolves to an existing `research.json`, so this guide is presented as a standalone survey and no locality entry is persisted.

---

New York City in the 1700s was a British colonial port town that kept no government birth, marriage, or death records whatsoever — churches, not the state, recorded vital events. The oldest and most important registers are the Dutch Reformed Church records (in Dutch, browse-only online through FamilySearch) and Trinity Church's Anglican registers (from 1697). For wills and estates, the Prerogative Court of New York handled all colonial-era probate, and the New-York Historical Society's published Abstracts of Wills series (1665–1800) is the standard finding aid. Tax assessment lists by ward are the only census substitute before the first federal census in 1790. Major physical repositories are the New York City Municipal Archives, the New York State Archives in Albany, the New-York Historical Society, and the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society — most colonial-era material is not online and requires in-person or written access.

If you want to move from this survey to a structured research plan targeting a specific family or question, that would be the natural next step.

Here is the locality guide's full response:

---

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## The Short Answer on Disasters and Substitutes

New Orleans in the early 1800s is one of the most disaster-affected archival environments in American genealogy — but it is not as bare as the fires might suggest.

### What Was Destroyed
- **Great Fire of 1788 (March 21):** ~856 buildings destroyed, including the original St. Louis Cathedral. Church and civil records created before that date were substantially lost.
- **Great Fire of 1794 (December 8):** A second catastrophic fire again put reconstructed records at risk.
- **Ongoing water damage:** Repeated flooding and humidity throughout the period damaged physical archives over time.
- **Epidemic disruption:** During major yellow fever outbreaks (especially 1832 and 1853), civil functions partially broke down, leaving sparse court and administrative records in those months.

### What Survived and Where to Find It

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) | Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; partially digitized on FamilySearch collection 1612905 (~987,654 records, indexed + images) |
| **Notarial acts** (property deeds, estate inventories, manumissions, wills, contracts) | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages from 1734); one browse-only FamilySearch volume covers 1803–1820 |
| **Spanish colonial padrones and administrative records** — copies survived in Spain when New Orleans copies burned | Archivo General de Indias, Seville (microfilm copies at some US partner libraries) |
| **Succession (probate) records** | Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives; FamilySearch collection 2078341 (~456,789 records, indexed) |
| **Federal census records** | 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 — indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **Passenger arrival lists** (1820 onward) | NARA RG 36; digitized on Ancestry |
| **City directories** (from 1820s) | New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection — best substitute for off-census years |

### The Core Strategy

Since Louisiana had **no statewide civil vital registration until 1914**, researchers must run three parallel tracks:

1. **Church registers** — The functional equivalent of birth, marriage, and death certificates. St. Louis Cathedral registered baptisms of *all* persons regardless of legal status, including enslaved persons.
2. **Notarial acts** — Every significant legal event was recorded here: property sales, estate inventories, manumissions, marriage contracts, wills. Duplicates were sometimes stored separately, which is why many survived when local copies burned.
3. **Federal records** — Census, passenger lists, military records, and federal land patents.

When a local record is missing, the first question to ask is: *Was a duplicate filed elsewhere?* For the Spanish colonial period especially, check the Archivo General de Indias in Seville — padrones (household censuses) and military lists taken under Spanish rule (1763–1803) partially survive there even when the New Orleans copy was lost.

---

This guide has been saved to the project as **loc_001**. The next step would be building a research plan targeting your specific ancestors within this framework, starting with the church registers and notarial acts.

quirks: Louisiana uses parishes (not counties) as its primary civil subdivision; New Orleans is coextensive with Orleans Parish. All courthouse and civil record searches should target Orleans Parish, not a county.
Louisiana follows civil law (Napoleonic Code), not common law. Probate is called 'succession'; guardianship is called 'tutorship'. Search Louisiana Probate Records for both.

Two catastrophic fires struck New Orleans in 1788 and 1794, destroying most colonial-era built structures and many records created before those dates. Most surviving pre-1800 records are church registers.

St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) begin in 1731 but have gaps due to the 1788 and 1794 fires. These are the primary substitute for missing civil vital records before statewide registration.

Statewide civil vital registration in Louisiana did not begin until 1914 at the state level. For the early 1800s, church registers at St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes are the only vital record series.

The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734. Notarial acts cover property sales, successions, contracts, manumissions, and slave sales — they are the backbone of early New Orleans research. The one FamilySearch digitized volume (image group 004990115) covers 1803–1820 and is browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) in French and English.

Records created under Spanish colonial rule (1763–1803) are in Spanish. Records from the French period (to 1763) are in French. Notarial acts through much of the early American period remain in French. Researchers must be able to read both languages or use translators.
The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records including legislative acts, governor's papers, and some court records.

For enslaved and free persons of color, sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral recorded baptisms regardless of legal status and are often the only surviving record. Notarial acts record manumissions and are essential for tracing free Black families.

Yellow fever epidemics repeatedly struck New Orleans throughout the early 1800s (major outbreaks in 1804, 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1853). Burial registers at St. Louis Cathedral spiked dramatically during epidemic years and are the main mortality record for this period.

Federal census records exist for New Orleans: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860. The 1810 and 1820 censuses list heads of household only. Slave schedules (non-indexed) begin with 1850. The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationwide.

New Orleans was a major port of entry. NARA holds passenger arrival lists for New Orleans from 1820 onward (Record Group 36). Earlier arrivals (1803–1819) are sparsely documented. Quarterly abstracts of passengers are in NARA M259.

Louisiana land grants prior to statehood were made by Spain and France. Confirmed grants are in the records of the U.S. General Land Office (BLM GLO website). The Louisiana State Land Office holds original Spanish and French colonial land grants.

Neighboring jurisdictions sharing a border with Orleans Parish include Jefferson Parish (west/south), St. Bernard Parish (east/southeast), and St. Tammany Parish (north across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near those borders may have generated records in those parishes as well.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Orleans Parish established 1807 from the Territory of Orleans (formed 1804 after the Louisiana Purchase, 1803). Louisiana achieved statehood 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are coextensive)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804–1812); State of Louisiana (1812–present)
- **Population during period:** No tool data returned for this place; census records exist for 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860. New Orleans was the largest city in the South by the 1840s and one of the largest in the US.
- **Economy:** Port commerce, cotton and sugar trade, banking, shipping. New Orleans was the premier port of the Mississippi River valley.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, Anglo-Americans (arriving after 1803), free persons of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African Americans, Irish and German immigrants (large waves from the 1830s–1850s), and smaller numbers of Italians and other Europeans.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral the seat of the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas, reorganized as the Diocese of New Orleans 1829), Protestant denominations arriving with Anglo-American settlers after 1803, Jewish congregation (established 1828).
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; territorial reorganization 1804–1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics (1804, 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1853 among the worst); major influx of Irish and German immigrants 1830s–1850s. Note: the two great fires of 1788 and 1794 predate this period but destroyed most records created before them.

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans as a city predates this period (founded 1718). The Territory of Orleans was organized 1804 from the Louisiana Purchase territory. Orleans Parish was legally established 1807 and has remained coextensive with the city throughout the period.
- No boundary changes within the period materially affect which jurisdiction holds records. Records created before 1803 (territorial) are in US custody or church custody; records created 1803–1812 are territorial; records from 1812 onward are state/parish.
- The city was divided into three municipalities 1836–1852 (First, Second, Third), each with its own council. Some municipal administrative records reflect this division; court and church records do not.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did not have statewide civil vital registration until 1914. During the early 1800s there was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths at the state or parish level comparable to what was established elsewhere.
- **What exists:** Church sacramental registers are the functional vital records for this period (see Church Records below). Some marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the parish level from the territorial period onward.
- **Where held:** Church registers at St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes; some civil marriage records at the Orleans Parish Clerk of Court.
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed records predating those events. Gaps in sacramental registers exist through the early 1800s as a result.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral registers (from 1731 with gaps); notarial acts (record marriages by contract); newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); Protestant congregations established after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations at St. Louis Cathedral from 1731 (with fire-related gaps). These registers are the single most important genealogical source for early New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives; FamilySearch has digitized some of these registers within collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925).
- **Language:** French and Spanish through much of the period; English records increase after 1803 but French remains common through the 1840s.
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 is indexed (987,654 records, 493,827 images). Check also the Archdiocese of New Orleans directly for records not yet digitized.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 (heads of household only; all household members listed 1850 onward), 1850, 1860. Slave schedules (non-indexed images) begin 1850.
- **State/territorial census:** Louisiana conducted some local enumerations in the territorial period; coverage is incomplete.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. The 1890 census is destroyed nationwide — substitute with city directories and other local records.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses 'succession' for probate (wills and intestate estates), 'tutorship' for guardianship, and 'interdiction' for incompetency proceedings. Inventories of estates are often extremely detailed and name heirs, creditors, and property including enslaved persons.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) covers the full period; 456,789 records, 228,394 images.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (successor to earlier district courts); Louisiana State Archives for older records.
- **Note:** Because Louisiana follows civil law, probate records are structured differently from common-law states. An intestate succession (no will) still generates a court file with an inventory — search for both.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot system in older areas plus the US rectangular survey system for later surveys.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish and French colonial grants were confirmed by the US after 1803. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website holds federal land patents. The Louisiana State Land Office holds colonial grants.
- **Types:** Notarial acts are the primary mechanism for recording property sales — deeds in Louisiana are notarial acts. Tax records (assessment rolls) also survive for many years.
- **Date range:** Notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center date to 1734. FamilySearch has one digitized volume of notarial acts covering 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, browse-only in French and English — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical and some digital); Louisiana State Land Office; BLM GLO website for federal patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War 1846–1848.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Record Group 15 for pensions, RG 94 for service records). Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives. Bounty land warrants (War of 1812 veterans) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (subscription) has digitized many War of 1812 service records and pension files.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 (1854), Cypress Grove Cemetery (1840), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833). New Orleans uses above-ground tombs due to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave has partial coverage. Some sexton records survive at the individual cemetery or the Archdiocese archives.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in St. Louis Cathedral registers are the primary record for Catholic burials. Protestant burial registers are held by individual congregations.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (from 1804), Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French-language, 1794–1814), the New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans (bilingual, from 1827), the Daily Picayune (from 1837).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Library; Tulane University; Newspapers.com (subscription) has digitized issues of several New Orleans papers. The Library of Congress Chronicling America project has some holdings.
- **Content value:** Vital notices (deaths, marriages), legal notices (estate settlements, property sales, sheriff's sales), ship arrivals, and community news. French-language papers are essential for the Creole community through at least the 1840s.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was a major port of entry, second only to New York for immigrant arrivals by the 1840s–1850s.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (RG 36) from 1820 onward. Quarterly abstracts 1803–1819 on NARA microfilm M259. Naturalization records (declarations of intention and petitions) filed in various courts — Orleans Parish district courts, US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana.
- **Where held:** NARA (online via Ancestry and FamilySearch for federal census arrivals); Ancestry holds the New Orleans passenger lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists name all persons aboard including infants. Examine the full manifest for the whole family. Pre-1820 arrivals are poorly documented — substitute with notarial acts, church records, and city directories.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Louisiana assessment rolls (property and personal); Orleans Parish tax records.
- **Date range:** Some assessment rolls survive from the territorial period onward.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; some are at the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection.
- **Substitute value:** Can stand in for missing census years; the 1830s–1840s rolls can help locate a person between census years.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts (all types):** Beyond property transfers, notarial acts record business contracts, partnerships, manumissions of enslaved persons, wills (in Louisiana a will may be notarial), apprenticeships, and powers of attorney. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the primary repository. This is often the richest source in the archive for early New Orleans research.
- **Records of enslaved persons:** Notarial acts record slave sales and manumissions by name. St. Louis Cathedral baptismal registers record the baptisms of enslaved persons. Succession inventories enumerate enslaved persons by name, age, and sometimes origin. These are the primary sources for tracing African American ancestry in this period.
- **City directories:** New Orleans directories begin in the 1820s. They place individuals at a specific address and give occupation — valuable in off-census years.
- **Published local histories:** Several 19th-century histories of Louisiana and New Orleans (e.g., Charles Gayarré's History of Louisiana) reprint early records and name founding families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905; ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054; ~567,890 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341; ~456,789 records); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892; ~2,345,678 records, index only); Notarial Acts volume 004990115 (1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (all years); New Orleans passenger arrival lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Partial cemetery inscription coverage | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists RG 36; military records RG 15, RG 94 | Free / in-person |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage note:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for this place and period (totalResults: 1). This is almost certainly not the complete picture — it reflects the current digitization and cataloguing state of FamilySearch's holdings for Orleans Parish specifically. Additional material may exist in the broader Louisiana state collections and under related place names. The record counts in the four FamilySearch collections above are figures returned by the tool; they should not be treated as verified totals.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; partial digital access via their website |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral registers and other parish records | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial/state court records, legislative records, some parish records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) files, civil court records | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Collection | City directories, local newspapers, assessment rolls, local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Plantation records, business papers, local manuscript collections | In-person by appointment |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, maps, photographs | In-person; some digitized |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal court records for Louisiana, including naturalizations | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts beyond the single 1803–1820 FamilySearch volume (image group 004990115) are physical-only or accessible only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.
- The majority of Orleans Parish civil court files (successions, tutorships, interdictions) are physical only at the courthouse or state archives.
- Assessment rolls and tax records are largely physical at the Louisiana State Archives and New Orleans Public Library.
- Pre-1820 passenger arrival records are sparse and largely physical at NARA or on microfilm only.
- St. Louis Cathedral registers not yet included in collection 1612905 are physical at the Archdiocese archives.
- Protestant congregation registers are held by individual churches or their denominational archives — no centralized online index.

## Known record losses

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Orleans Parish established 1807 from the Territory of Orleans (itself organized 1804 after the Louisiana Purchase of 1803). Louisiana achieved statehood 1812.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are coextensive)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804-1812); State of Louisiana (1812-present)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this specific place. Federal census records survive for 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860. By the 1840s New Orleans was the largest city in the South and among the largest in the nation.
- **Economy:** Port commerce, cotton and sugar trade, banking, and shipping. New Orleans was the premier port of the Mississippi River valley.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, Anglo-Americans (arriving in large numbers after 1803), free persons of color (gens de couleur libres, one of the largest such communities in North America), enslaved African Americans, Irish and German immigrants (major waves from the 1830s through 1850s), and smaller Italian and other European communities.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral was the seat of the Diocese of Louisiana and the Floridas, reorganized as the Diocese of New Orleans 1829), Protestant congregations established after 1803 with the Anglo-American influx, Jewish congregation established 1828.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; territorial organization 1804-1812; Battle of New Orleans January 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics (major outbreaks 1804, 1817, 1819, 1822, 1832, 1853); large Irish and German immigration 1830s-1850s. The two great fires of 1788 and 1794 predate this period but destroyed most records created before them.

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans was founded 1718. The Territory of Orleans was organized 1804; Orleans Parish established 1807 and has remained coextensive with the city throughout the target period.
- No boundary changes within 1800-1860 materially affect which jurisdiction holds records. Records created before 1803 are in US federal or church custody; records 1803-1812 are territorial; records from 1812 onward are state/parish.
- The city was divided into three municipalities 1836-1852 (First, Second, Third municipalities), each with its own council. Some municipal administrative records reflect this division, but court and church records do not.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did not have statewide civil vital registration until 1914. No civil birth, marriage, or death registration existed at the state or parish level during the early 1800s in the modern sense.
- **What exists:** Church sacramental registers are the functional vital records for this entire period (see Church Records below). Some civil marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the parish level from the territorial period onward, but coverage is incomplete.
- **Where held:** Church registers at St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes; some civil marriage records at the Orleans Parish Clerk of Court.
- **Gaps:** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed records predating those events, with continuing gaps into the early 1800s.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers; notarial acts (which record marriage contracts); newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant throughout the period); Protestant denominations established after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations at St. Louis Cathedral from 1731 (with fire-related gaps). These registers are the single most important genealogical source for early New Orleans.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives. FamilySearch has digitized a portion within collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925), which is indexed and carries approximately 987,654 records and 493,827 images.
- **Language:** French and Spanish through much of the period; English increases after 1803 but French remains common into the 1840s. Researchers must be able to read both or use a translator.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the FamilySearch portion (collection 1612905). Records not yet in that collection are physical-only at the Archdiocese archives.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 (heads of household only), 1850, 1860 (full household listing). Slave schedules (non-indexed images) begin 1850.
- **State/territorial census:** Some local enumerations survive from the territorial period; coverage is incomplete and not centrally indexed.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) were taken under Spanish rule and partially survive in the Archivo General de Indias, Seville -- a valuable supplement for families present before 1803.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed on both Ancestry and FamilySearch. The 1890 federal census is destroyed nationwide; substitute with city directories and other local records. Slave schedules must be browsed image-by-image.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana uses "succession" (not "probate") for estate proceedings -- both testate (will filed) and intestate (no will). "Tutorship" replaces guardianship. "Interdiction" covers incompetency. Estate inventories are often extremely detailed and name heirs, creditors, and enslaved persons by name and sometimes age and origin.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984) covers the full target period with approximately 456,789 records and 228,394 images. Indexed + images.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (successor to earlier district courts); Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge for older records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system in older areas; US rectangular survey for later surveys.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish and French colonial grants were confirmed by the US after 1803. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website holds confirmed federal patents. The Louisiana State Land Office holds colonial grants.
- **Types:** Notarial acts are the primary instrument for recording property sales in Louisiana -- a deed here is a notarial act, not a separate deed book as in common-law states. Tax assessment rolls also survive for many years.
- **Date range:** Notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center date to 1734. FamilySearch has one digitized volume covering 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images). This volume is browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, and in mixed French and English. It must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (physical; partial digital access via their website); Louisiana State Land Office; BLM GLO website for federal patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (culminating in the Battle of New Orleans, January 8, 1815); Mexican-American War 1846-1848.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Record Group 15 for pensions, RG 94 for service records). Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives. Bounty land warrants (War of 1812 veterans) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (subscription) has digitized many War of 1812 service records and pension files.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (established 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 (1854), Cypress Grove Cemetery (1840), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833). New Orleans uses above-ground tombs due to the high water table; many family vaults hold multiple interments.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave has partial coverage.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers are the primary Catholic burial record. Protestant burial registers are held by individual congregations. Sexton records, where they survive, are at individual cemeteries or the Archdiocese archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Louisiana Gazette (from 1804); Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French-language, 1794-1814); New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orleans (bilingual, from 1827); Daily Picayune (from 1837).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Library; Tulane University; Newspapers.com (subscription) has digitized issues of several New Orleans papers; Library of Congress Chronicling America project has some holdings.
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate settlements, property sales, sheriff's sales), ship arrivals, and community news. French-language papers are essential for the Creole community through at least the 1840s.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was a major port of entry -- second only to New York for immigrant arrivals by the 1840s-1850s.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (RG 36) from 1820 onward. Quarterly abstracts for 1803-1819 on NARA microfilm M259. Naturalization records (declarations of intention and petitions) filed in various courts: Orleans Parish district courts, US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana.
- **Where held:** NARA (online via Ancestry for New Orleans passenger lists); Ancestry holds the digitized arrival lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists name all persons aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents -- examine the full manifest for all family members. Pre-1820 arrivals are sparsely documented; substitute with notarial acts, church records, and city directories.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Louisiana assessment rolls (property and personal property); Orleans Parish tax records.
- **Date range:** Some assessment rolls survive from the territorial period onward.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; some at the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection.
- **Substitute value:** Can stand in for missing census years. Assessment rolls from the 1830s-1840s can help locate a person between census enumerations.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts (all types):** Beyond property transfers, notarial acts record business contracts, partnerships, manumissions of enslaved persons, wills (a Louisiana will may be a notarial act), apprenticeships, and powers of attorney. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734. This is often the richest source in the archive for early New Orleans research for any population group.
- **Records of enslaved and free persons of color:** Notarial acts record slave sales and manumissions by name. St. Louis Cathedral baptismal registers record the baptisms of enslaved persons regardless of legal status. Succession inventories enumerate enslaved persons by name, age, and sometimes origin. These are the primary sources for tracing African American ancestry in this period.
- **City directories:** New Orleans directories begin in the 1820s. They place an individual at a specific address and give occupation -- valuable in off-census years.
- **Published local histories:** 19th-century histories of Louisiana and New Orleans (e.g., Charles Gayarre's History of Louisiana) reprint early records and name founding families.

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905; ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images, indexed); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (collection 1798054; ~567,890 records, indexed); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341; ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images, indexed); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (collection 1543892; ~2,345,678 records, index only, no images); Notarial Acts 1803-1820 (volume 004990115, 167 images, browse-only) | Free |

| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists RG 36; military records RG 15, RG 94 | Free (online finding aids; some records in-person) |

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); Mexican-American War 1846–1848.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Record Group 15 for pensions, RG 94 for service records). Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives. Bounty land warrants (War of 1812 veterans) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (subscription) has digitized many War of 1812 service records and pension files.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 (1854), Cypress Grove Cemetery (1840), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833). New Orleans uses above-ground tombs due to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave has partial coverage. Some sexton records survive at the individual cemetery or the Archdiocese archives.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in St. Louis Cathedral registers are the primary record for Catholic burials. Protestant burial registers are held by individual congregations.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (from 1804), Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French-language, 1794–1814), the New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans (bilingual, from 1827), the Daily Picayune (from 1837).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Library; Tulane University; Newspapers.com (subscription) has digitized issues of several New Orleans papers. The Library of Congress Chronicling America project has some holdings.
- **Content value:** Vital notices (deaths, marriages), legal notices (estate settlements, property sales, sheriff's sales), ship arrivals, and community news. French-language papers are essential for the Creole community through at least the 1840s.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was a major port of entry, second only to New York for immigrant arrivals by the 1840s–1850s.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA (RG 36) from 1820 onward. Quarterly abstracts 1803–1819 on NARA microfilm M259. Naturalization records (declarations of intention and petitions) filed in various courts — Orleans Parish district courts, US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana.
- **Where held:** NARA (online via Ancestry and FamilySearch for federal census arrivals); Ancestry holds the New Orleans passenger lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists name all persons aboard including infants. Examine the full manifest for the whole family. Pre-1820 arrivals are poorly documented — substitute with notarial acts, church records, and city directories.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Louisiana assessment rolls (property and personal); Orleans Parish tax records.
- **Date range:** Some assessment rolls survive from the territorial period onward.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; some are at the New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection.
- **Substitute value:** Can stand in for missing census years; the 1830s–1840s rolls can help locate a person between census years.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts (all types):** Beyond property transfers, notarial acts record business contracts, partnerships, manumissions of enslaved persons, wills (in Louisiana a will may be notarial), apprenticeships, and powers of attorney. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the primary repository. This is often the richest source in the archive for early New Orleans research.
- **Records of enslaved persons:** Notarial acts record slave sales and manumissions by name. St. Louis Cathedral baptismal registers record the baptisms of enslaved persons. Succession inventories enumerate enslaved persons by name, age, and sometimes origin. These are the primary sources for tracing African American ancestry in this period.
- **City directories:** New Orleans directories begin in the 1820s. They place individuals at a specific address and give occupation — valuable in off-census years.
- **Published local histories:** Several 19th-century histories of Louisiana and New Orleans (e.g., Charles Gayarré's History of Louisiana) reprint early records and name founding families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905; ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054; ~567,890 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341; ~456,789 records); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892; ~2,345,678 records, index only); Notarial Acts volume 004990115 (1803–1820, 167 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (all years); New Orleans passenger arrival lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Partial cemetery inscription coverage | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists RG 36; military records RG 15, RG 94 | Free / in-person |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage note:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for this place and period (totalResults: 1). This is almost certainly not the complete picture — it reflects the current digitization and cataloguing state of FamilySearch's holdings for Orleans Parish specifically. Additional material may exist in the broader Louisiana state collections and under related place names. The record counts in the four FamilySearch collections above are figures returned by the tool; they should not be treated as verified totals.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; partial digital access via their website |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral registers and other parish records | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial/state court records, legislative records, some parish records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) files, civil court records | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Collection | City directories, local newspapers, assessment rolls, local histories | In-person; some digitized |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Plantation records, business papers, local manuscript collections | In-person by appointment |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, maps, photographs | In-person; some digitized |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal court records for Louisiana, including naturalizations | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts beyond the single 1803–1820 FamilySearch volume (image group 004990115) are physical-only or accessible only at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.
- The majority of Orleans Parish civil court files (successions, tutorships, interdictions) are physical only at the courthouse or state archives.
- Assessment rolls and tax records are largely physical at the Louisiana State Archives and New Orleans Public Library.
- Pre-1820 passenger arrival records are sparse and largely physical at NARA or on microfilm only.
- St. Louis Cathedral registers not yet included in collection 1612905 are physical at the Archdiocese archives.
- Protestant congregation registers are held by individual churches or their denominational archives — no centralized online index.

## Known record losses
- **Great Fire of 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings in New Orleans on March 21, 1788. Church records and civil records created before that date were substantially lost. St. Louis Cathedral itself was destroyed and rebuilt.
- **Great Fire of 1794:** A second catastrophic fire on December 8, 1794 destroyed another large portion of the city. Records that had been reconstructed or survived 1788 were again put at risk.
- **What survived:** The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral have partial survival from 1731 onward, with identifiable gaps. Notarial acts at the Notarial Archives have significant survival because notarial originals and copies were sometimes kept in separate locations. Spanish colonial administrative records partially survived in both New Orleans and in the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain — a critical source for the Spanish period (1763–1803).
- **Substitutes for fire losses:** (1) Archivo General de Indias, Seville — holds Spanish colonial records for Louisiana including census-type enumerations (padrones), military records, and land grants; (2) reconstructed church registers at the Archdiocese archives; (3) notarial acts that survived in duplicate; (4) records held at the territorial/federal level in Washington that predate local losses.
- **Yellow fever mortality:** The epidemic years created enormous gaps in ordinary record-keeping as civil functions broke down. Burial records spike but administrative and court records may be sparse or absent for those months.
- **Flood and hurricane damage:** Repeated flooding throughout the period damaged physical archives. No single catastrophic archival flood is documented for this period comparable to the 1788/1794 fires, but cumulative water damage to paper records is a known problem.

## Research tips
- New Orleans research in the early 1800s requires three parallel tracks: church registers, notarial acts, and federal records. Civil vital registration did not exist; these three series are the functional equivalent. (Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- Louisiana's civil law system means terminology differs from other US states: look for 'succession' not 'probate,' 'tutorship' not 'guardianship.' This affects how you search FamilySearch collection 2078341.
- For Spanish colonial ancestors (those in New Orleans before 1803), check the Archivo General de Indias in Seville. The padrones (household censuses) taken under Spanish rule are detailed nominal lists and partially survive.
- Records are in French or Spanish through much of this period. Even English-speaking researchers will encounter French-language church registers, notarial acts, and newspapers. Basic reading ability or a translator is needed.
- Women in Louisiana civil law records may appear under their birth surname even after marriage. Search for both the birth name and the married name.
- Enslaved and free persons of color generated records in both the church (baptismal registers at St. Louis Cathedral) and the notarial system (manumission acts, sale acts). Do not limit a search to civil or federal records for African American ancestors — the notarial and church tracks are often the only ones that exist.
- When a record is missing, check whether a copy was filed in a second location. Notarial acts were often filed in duplicate. Colonial records may survive in Spain even when the New Orleans copy was lost.
- City directories for New Orleans begin in the 1820s and are available at the New Orleans Public Library. They are the best substitute for census years when a person cannot be found in the federal census.
- For immigrant ancestors arriving at New Orleans, check NARA passenger lists from 1820 onward (digitized on Ancestry). For earlier arrivals (1803–1819), the quarterly abstracts on NARA microfilm M259 are the main source, but coverage is sparse.
- The three-municipality division of New Orleans (1836–1852) does not affect church or court records but may affect the attribution of some municipal administrative records to a specific arrondissement.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Boston was a well-established city within Suffolk County by the 1840s. The port drove the city's economy, and by 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the surge from the Great Famine (1845–1852). No significant boundary changes affected record-keeping during this period.

---

## Key Record Types

### 1. Passenger Lists (Arrival Manifests) — Start Here
- **What:** Customs passenger lists under the Steerage Act of 1819 — name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin for every passenger
- **FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312) — indexed + images; [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312)
- **Volume:** FamilySearch volume 003345210 covers Port of Boston 1840–1850 (389 images); nearly un-indexed but **full-text searchable**
- **Originals:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), NARA RG 36
- **Also on:** Ancestry.com
- **Warning:** These manifests are thin — no town of origin, no relatives' names. They confirm arrival but rarely point you back to a specific village.

### 2. Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Database — Critical for Irish Immigrants
- **What:** Irish immigrants placed ads in the *Boston Pilot* newspaper seeking lost relatives, often naming their Irish townland or parish of origin — information missing from the customs lists
- **Why it matters:** This is one of the only 1840s sources that records a specific place of origin in Ireland
- **Access:** Indexed database, previously at https://infowanted.bc.edu/ (verify current URL)

### 3. Naturalization Records
- **What:** Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization, filed in any court of record (Suffolk County Superior Court, Probate Court, U.S. Circuit Court, U.S. District Court)
- **FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213); [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213)
- **Key tip:** A man who arrived in 1845 could declare intention in 1846 but couldn't petition until 1851 — search 1840–1860, not just the arrival year. Also search all court types, not just one.

### 4. Church Records — Often More Complete Than Civil Records
- **Key parishes for Irish immigrants:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's Church (East Boston, opened 1844 — right at the immigrant landing areas); additional Catholic parishes established through the decade
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Custodian:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Braintree, MA) — contact at https://www.bostoncatholic.org/archives
- **FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection 1921657); [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — coverage of specific Boston Catholic parishes should be verified

### 5. Federal & State Census Records
- **1840 federal census:** Names heads of household only — limited usefulness for immigrants
- **1850 federal census:** Names every individual with age, sex, birthplace (country level), and occupation — far more useful
- **1855 Massachusetts state census:** Names every person; often includes more detailed nativity information; held at Massachusetts Archives
- **Mortality schedules (1850):** Name individuals who died in the prior year

### 6. Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Massachusetts began statewide registration in 1842, but **compliance was uneven in the 1840s** — church records often predate and are more complete than civil ones
- **FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection 2061550); [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)
- **Also at:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); town clerk offices

### 7. Massachusetts State Alien Passenger Records
- Separate from federal customs lists — Massachusetts passed its own alien passenger laws requiring ship masters to report passengers; may contain additional detail
- **Where:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston (not confirmed digitized)

### 8. City Directories
- Annual or biennial listings by name, occupation, and street address — fill gaps between census years (1840–1850)
- **Where:** Boston Public Library; many years on Ancestry.com; some on Google Books

### 9. Probate & Court Records
- **FamilySearch:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection 1678901); [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- Most useful for the 1850s–1870s for 1840s arrivals (immigrants who arrived with little property)

### 10. Newspapers
- **The Boston Pilot:** Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper from 1836 — death notices, marriage announcements, Missing Persons ads
- **Ship arrival notices:** *Boston Daily Atlas*, *Boston Post*, and other papers named vessels and sometimes passengers
- **Access:** Boston Public Library (microfilm); Newspapers.com; GenealogyBank (subscription)

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger lists, naturalizations, vital records, church records, probate | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Customs lists, federal censuses, city directories | Subscription |
| Boston Pilot Missing Persons DB | Irish Missing Persons ads, indexed | Free (verify URL) |
| Fold3.com | Military service records & pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank | Boston Pilot, Boston papers | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists (NARA RG 36); pre-1906 federal court naturalization records |
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | State vital records; state alien passenger records; some court records |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Braintree, MA) | Catholic parish registers — Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and others |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (Boston) | Deed books from colonial era through present |
| Boston Public Library | City directories; newspapers on microfilm |

---

## Records NOT Online
- Massachusetts state alien passenger records (at MA Archives; digitization unconfirmed)
- Full run of *The Boston Pilot* (partial digitization only)
- Most Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers for specific parishes
- Boston city health records and almshouse/poorhouse records from the 1840s

## Known Gaps
No major courthouse fire affected Boston's 1840s records. However:
- The customs passenger lists are **structurally thin by law** — town or parish of origin was not required and almost never recorded. This is not record loss; it's a design limitation.
- Some early Catholic parish registers may have been lost before the Archdiocese consolidated holdings — contact the Archives directly to confirm survival for a specific parish.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database.** It's the single most powerful bridge between a Boston arrival and an Irish townland or parish — information you will not find on the customs manifest.

2. **Search both the indexed collection AND the raw volume on FamilySearch.** The name index (collection 1784312) is the first stop; volume 003345210 is nearly un-indexed but full-text searchable — try a ship name or neighbor's surname to surface surrounding pages.

3. **Naturalization declarations predate petitions by 5+ years.** Search the full 1840–1860 window, and search all court types (Suffolk County Superior, Probate, U.S. Circuit, U.S. District).

4. **Church records should be searched in parallel with civil records, not as a fallback.** Civil registration compliance was imperfect in the 1840s; the church baptism or marriage is often earlier and more detailed.

5. **Use the 1850 census, not the 1840.** The 1840 census names heads of household only. The 1850 census names everyone — it's far more useful for placing 1840s arrivals in a family context.

6. **Check the 1855 Massachusetts state census.** It's closer in time to the arrival decade than the 1860 federal census and often includes more detailed nativity information.

7. **Trace movement inland.** Irish and other immigrants arriving in the 1840s often moved to Worcester County, Middlesex County, or further west along the rail lines. If an ancestor disappears from Boston records, those are the next stops.

---
