---

# Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1860–1900) — Locality Guide

## Jurisdiction overview
Pittsburgh is the county seat of Allegheny County (formed 1788). During the late 1800s steel boom, the city attracted massive immigrant labor — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Hungarian, Italian, Irish, German, and Welsh workers poured into mill neighborhoods. Carnegie Steel's operations dominated the economy through the 1870s–1890s.

**Critical boundary note:** **Allegheny City** (today's North Side) was a completely separate municipality with its own court and records until it was annexed into Pittsburgh in 1907. A family living on the north bank appears in *Allegheny City* records, not Pittsburgh's. The Borough of Homestead is also a separate municipality within Allegheny County.

---

## Records for the 1860–1900 window

### Vital records
Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration until 1906**. For this window:
- **County marriage registers** begin 1885. FamilySearch collections:
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — 524,000 records, fully indexed
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — 312,000 records, indexed
- **Births and deaths** are not in any civil register before 1906. Alternatives: baptism/burial registers, city directories, newspaper obituaries.
- Death certificates (1906+) are indexed on FamilySearch and are useful for people who died shortly after the target period.

### Church records
- **Catholic parishes were organized by national origin, not geography.** A Slovak family attended a Slovak parish; the Irish or German parish register is the wrong place. Identify ethnic origin from the 1900 census before approaching any parish register.
- Denominations: Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, German Lutheran, Eastern Orthodox (Slovak, Serbian, Ukrainian), Jewish congregations.
- Held at: Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives (Catholic); individual parishes; some microfilmed by FamilySearch (browse-only, limited indexing).

### Census records
- 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses: **fully indexed and free on FamilySearch**.
- **The 1890 census was destroyed nationally.** Bridge this gap with city directories, church records, and county tax rolls.
- The **1900 census** is the richest single document for immigrant mill workers: it records year of immigration, years in the US, and citizenship status.
- Mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880) partially compensate for absent civil death registration.

### Occupational and industrial records *(the steel-era core)*
- **Company employment records** (Carnegie Steel, U.S. Steel, etc.) survive only in fragments. Primary repositories:
  - **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — in-person or correspondence only
  - **Rivers of Steel archives** (Homestead, PA) — in-person; contact for access
  - Neither is digitized or indexed online.
- **City directories:** The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds annual Pittsburgh directories from the 1810s onward. Each entry lists name, address, and occupation. For 1860–1900 — especially the 1890 gap — a directory entry is often the only year-by-year evidence for a mill-worker family.
- **Union membership records:** Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers (founded 1876). Fragmentary survival; contact the United Steelworkers archives and the Heinz History Center.
- **Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics factory inspection reports:** Published annually from 1872, naming establishments and sometimes key workers. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) and some research libraries.
- **Coroner records for mill accidents:** Allegheny County Coroner's records document workplace fatalities. Held at the Allegheny County courthouse; not digitized.

### Immigration and naturalization
- Most immigrants arrived via New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island from 1892), Baltimore, or Philadelphia.
- **Naturalization records** (pre-1906) could be filed in any court of record — Allegheny County Common Pleas, other state courts, or federal courts. The Declaration of Intention and the later Petition may be in different courts, filed years apart.
- FamilySearch has a Pennsylvania naturalization volume (1790–1915, 351 images, partially indexed). NARA Mid-Atlantic (Philadelphia) holds federal-court naturalization records.
- Passenger manifests: indexed and searchable via Ancestry, FamilySearch, and NARA.

### Other key record types
| Record | Held at | Digitized? |
|---|---|---|
| Probate (wills, inventories) | Allegheny County courthouse; FamilySearch (3.2M images, browse-only) | Browse-only |
| Deeds / land records | Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds | Not broadly digitized |
| County property tax rolls | Courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives | Not digitized |
| Military (Civil War) | NARA; Fold3; PA State Archives | Indexed indexes; full files via NARA request |
| Cemetery records | FindAGrave (free); BillionGraves; sexton records at individual cemeteries | Partial online coverage |
| Newspaper obituaries/marriage notices | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription) | Partial |
| Ethnic-language newspapers | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | Microfilm; some online |

---

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County marriages 1885–1950 (indexed); Probate 1683–1994 (browse-only); Death certificates 1906+ (indexed); Naturalization records (partial) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1860–1900 (fully indexed) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War pension and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Pittsburgh-area cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Selected Pittsburgh newspaper runs | Subscription |

### Physical / correspondence
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company records, union records, immigration/industrial collections |
| **Rivers of Steel archives** (Homestead) | Steel-industry records, mill photographs, worker oral histories |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | Annual city directories (1810s–), local history, newspaper microfilm |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage records, probate, deeds, coroner records, court files |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Factory inspection reports, land warrants/patents, state records |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic** (Philadelphia) | Federal naturalization records, passenger manifests |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers |

---

## Research strategy for steel-era families

1. **Start with the 1900 census** — it gives immigration year, years in the US, and citizenship status. Use that to narrow the manifest search and the naturalization window.
2. **Identify ethnic/national origin** before approaching any Catholic church register. Parish registers are sorted by community, not neighborhood.
3. **Bridge the 1890 gap** with annual city directories at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh. These are the best annual-resolution evidence available for working-class families.
4. **Search both Pittsburgh and Allegheny City records** for families who lived on or moved to the North Side before 1907.
5. **Check all three naturalization court jurisdictions** (county, state, federal) — the Declaration of Intention and later Petition for Naturalization may be in different courts.
6. **For mill accidents and workplace deaths**, the Allegheny County Coroner's records are the primary source. These are physical-only at the courthouse.
7. **For industrial employment itself**, plan an in-person or correspondence visit to the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives. There is no online substitute.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from Westmoreland and Washington Counties; Pittsburgh incorporated 1816.
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data not returned by the place_population tool for this standardPlace. Wikipedia notes that Pittsburgh's rapid industrialization attracted massive immigrant labor from the 1870s onward, making it one of the fastest-growing urban counties in the US by 1900.
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing (Carnegie Steel and successor firms), iron production, glass, coal, and river commerce. The late 1800s were the peak of the steel boom.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Welsh, and English settlers from earlier decades; from the 1870s–1890s, large influxes of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Hungarian, Italian, and Jewish immigrants into mill neighborhoods.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes organized by nationality), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Lutheran (German), Eastern Orthodox (Slovak, Serbian, Ukrainian), Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892 (Carnegie Steel); Great Railroad Strike of 1877; rapid expansion of Carnegie Steel through the 1880s–1890s.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County has been stable since 1800. Allegheny City (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh) was a separate municipality until 1907, when it was annexed into Pittsburgh. Before 1907, Allegheny City had its own court and municipal records distinct from Pittsburgh's — check both sets for families living on the north bank.
- The neighboring city of Homestead (site of Carnegie's works) is in Allegheny County but was a separate borough with its own municipal records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, and deaths until 1906 (statewide level). For the 1860–1900 period, there is no mandatory civil registration system in effect at the state level.
- **What exists:** County marriage registers exist at the county level from 1885. The FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, 312,045 images) covers marriages at the county level beginning 1885. *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection 1571957, 312,045 records) and *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection 1502909, 198,765 records) provide additional coverage. Birth and death registration before 1906 was not systematically required — church records are the primary substitute.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse; FamilySearch (collections above, searchable by name for marriages); Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration for the 1860–1900 window. Death certificates begin statewide in 1906 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4.2 million records, fully indexed).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Baptism/burial registers of ethnic Catholic parishes, Protestant church registers, city directory death notices, newspaper obituaries.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes: Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, German), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, German Lutheran, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives of the Diocese of Pittsburgh for Catholic records; individual parishes for those not yet transferred; FamilySearch has microfilmed some series. The FamilySearch wiki search results confirm Catholic parishes are organized by ethnic community — identifying the ethnic group is the prerequisite step ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)).
- **Language:** Latin for pre-1900 Catholic sacramental records; Polish, Slovak, or German for registers kept in the vernacular of the congregation.
- **Access:** Partly microfilmed; not comprehensively indexed. Expect browse-only or physical-only access for many parish registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (fully available; 1890 destroyed nationally). All list occupation. The 1880 census added relationship to head of household. The 1900 census lists years of immigration and citizenship status — critical for immigrant steel workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the preceding year — useful for the pre-1906 death gap.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Access:** 1860–1900 federal censuses are fully indexed and available free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County from 1788.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills); FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images but 0% name-indexed, so browse-only.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images on FamilySearch. The 3 statewide-scope digitized volumes returned by volume_search include a probate volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Note:** Court minute books at the Allegheny County courthouse also record county business — road maintenance assignments, indigent relief payments — that name ordinary working people not party to any suit.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania uses metes and bounds (not the federal rectangular survey system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania was a state-land state; original grants and warrants were issued by the Commonwealth through the Pennsylvania Land Office. The *Pennsylvania Land and Property* FamilySearch wiki page was requested but returned only a generic page — specific Land Office details were not confirmed from that fetch.
- **Types:** Deeds (county recorder), warrants and patents (Pennsylvania State Archives), tax records (county).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds for post-formation deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for original warrants and patents; county tax assessment records at the courthouse.
- **Access:** Not broadly digitized for this period. Physical or microfilm access required for most deed and tax series.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant conflict for this population. Spanish-American War (1898) for those born in the 1870s–1880s.
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records at NARA; Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; state bounty records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and National Personnel Records Center); Fold3 (subscription, online) for Civil War pension and service indexes; Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Access:** Civil War pension index is indexed and searchable online via Fold3 and Ancestry. Full pension files require a NARA request.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (1844, nonsectarian), St. Mary's Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic parish cemeteries throughout mill neighborhoods.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com, free) has substantial Pittsburgh-area coverage. BillionGraves also indexes some local cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; not comprehensively digitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (founded 1786, continuous), Pittsburgh Press, Pittsburgh Dispatch, and ethnic-language papers (Polish, Slovak, Croatian dailies and weeklies serving mill communities).
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds extensive newspaper runs on microfilm. Newspapers.com (subscription) has digitized some Pittsburgh papers. The Library of Congress Chronicling America project has some Pennsylvania papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, strike coverage (Homestead 1892), legal notices, and employment announcements. Ethnic-language newspapers are often the only source for community-level events.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Immigrants to Pittsburgh's steel mills typically arrived through the Port of New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island 1892 onward), Baltimore, or Philadelphia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA); naturalization records (Allegheny County courthouse, Common Pleas Court, and federal courts — pre-1906 naturalization could be filed in any court of record); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization.
- **Naturalization access:** FamilySearch has a digitized Pennsylvania-level naturalization volume (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 1790–1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, English and German). The wiki search confirms the National Archives at Philadelphia holds federal-court naturalization records for this region ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)).

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from Westmoreland and Washington Counties; Pittsburgh incorporated 1816.
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this standardPlace. - **Economy:** Steel manufacturing (Carnegie Steel and successor firms), iron production, glass, coal, and river commerce. The late 1800s were the peak of the steel boom.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Welsh, and English settlers from earlier decades; from the 1870s-1890s, large influxes of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Hungarian, Italian, and Jewish immigrants into mill neighborhoods.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes organized by nationality), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, German Lutheran, Eastern Orthodox (Slovak, Serbian, Ukrainian), Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892 (Carnegie Steel); Great Railroad Strike of 1877; rapid expansion of Carnegie Steel through the 1880s-1890s.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County has been stable since 1800.
- **Allegheny City** (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh, now the North Side) was a separate municipality until 1907 when it was annexed into Pittsburgh. Before 1907, Allegheny City had its own court and municipal records entirely distinct from Pittsburgh's. Families living on the north bank appear in Allegheny City records, not Pittsburgh's.
- The borough of Homestead (site of Carnegie's flagship works) is in Allegheny County but was a separate municipality with its own records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906 (statewide level).   - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950* (collection 1571957) — 312,045 records, indexed
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900* (collection 1502909) — 198,765 records, indexed
  - Births and deaths before 1906 are not in any systematic civil register.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse; FamilySearch (marriage collections above, searchable by name); Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration for the target window. ### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, German), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, German Lutheran, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish.

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 are all fully available and indexed. The 1890 census was destroyed nationally. All enumerations list occupation. - **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.

### Probate and court records

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (fully available; 1890 destroyed nationally). All list occupation. The 1880 census added relationship to head of household. The 1900 census lists years of immigration and citizenship status — critical for immigrant steel workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the preceding year — useful for the pre-1906 death gap.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Access:** 1860–1900 federal censuses are fully indexed and available free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County from 1788.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills); FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images but 0% name-indexed, so browse-only.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images on FamilySearch. The 3 statewide-scope digitized volumes returned by volume_search include a probate volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Note:** Court minute books at the Allegheny County courthouse also record county business — road maintenance assignments, indigent relief payments — that name ordinary working people not party to any suit.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania uses metes and bounds (not the federal rectangular survey system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania was a state-land state; original grants and warrants were issued by the Commonwealth through the Pennsylvania Land Office. The *Pennsylvania Land and Property* FamilySearch wiki page was requested but returned only a generic page — specific Land Office details were not confirmed from that fetch.
- **Types:** Deeds (county recorder), warrants and patents (Pennsylvania State Archives), tax records (county).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds for post-formation deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for original warrants and patents; county tax assessment records at the courthouse.
- **Access:** Not broadly digitized for this period. Physical or microfilm access required for most deed and tax series.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant conflict for this population. Spanish-American War (1898) for those born in the 1870s–1880s.
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records at NARA; Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; state bounty records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and National Personnel Records Center); Fold3 (subscription, online) for Civil War pension and service indexes; Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Access:** Civil War pension index is indexed and searchable online via Fold3 and Ancestry. Full pension files require a NARA request.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (1844, nonsectarian), St. Mary's Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic parish cemeteries throughout mill neighborhoods.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com, free) has substantial Pittsburgh-area coverage. BillionGraves also indexes some local cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; not comprehensively digitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (founded 1786, continuous), Pittsburgh Press, Pittsburgh Dispatch, and ethnic-language papers (Polish, Slovak, Croatian dailies and weeklies serving mill communities).
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds extensive newspaper runs on microfilm. Newspapers.com (subscription) has digitized some Pittsburgh papers. The Library of Congress Chronicling America project has some Pennsylvania papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, strike coverage (Homestead 1892), legal notices, and employment announcements. Ethnic-language newspapers are often the only source for community-level events.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Immigrants to Pittsburgh's steel mills typically arrived through the Port of New York (Castle Garden before 1892, Ellis Island 1892 onward), Baltimore, or Philadelphia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA); naturalization records (Allegheny County courthouse, Common Pleas Court, and federal courts — pre-1906 naturalization could be filed in any court of record); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization.
- **Naturalization access:** FamilySearch has a digitized Pennsylvania-level naturalization volume (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 1790–1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, English and German). The wiki search confirms the National Archives at Philadelphia holds federal-court naturalization records for this region ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)).
- **The 1900 census** lists year of immigration and number of years in the US — use it to estimate an arrival window before searching manifests.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest page for siblings and accompanying family members when tracing a family group.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County tax records from 1788.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Can confirm a person's residence and rough economic status in years between census enumerations.

### Occupational and industrial records (steel-era focus)
This is the record class most distinctive to Pittsburgh research and the one with the most scattered survival.
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary. Carnegie Steel and successor U.S. Steel company records are not comprehensively preserved. The most significant surviving collections are held at the **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives** (Homestead, PA). Neither is digitized or indexed online — physical or correspondence access required ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward. These list each head of household by name, address, and occupation annually. For the 1860–1900 period, city directories are the single best tool for tracking a steel-worker family between census years.
- **Union membership records:** Records of the Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers (founded 1876) survive fragmentarily; contact the United Steelworkers archives and the Heinz History Center.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspection reports from 1872 onward, naming establishments and sometimes foremen or key workers. Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and available in some research libraries.
- **Accident and coroner records:** Mill accidents were common. Allegheny County Coroner's records document workplace fatalities and name the deceased, employer, and circumstances. Held at the Allegheny County courthouse; not digitized.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** See Occupational section above — essential for this research context.
- **School records:** Pittsburgh public school records (enrollment, attendance) held at the Pittsburgh Public Schools and the Pittsburgh City Archives; not digitized.
- **Hospital and institutional records:** Western Pennsylvania Hospital and other institutions admitted mill-injury patients; records vary in survival and access.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1885–1950 (524K records, indexed); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K records); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (199K records); Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records, indexed); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (partial index) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 — fully indexed) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War pension and service record indexes | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records for Pittsburgh-area cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Selected Pittsburgh newspaper runs | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger manifests, federal naturalization records, military records | Free finding aids; some records fee-based |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes total at the Pennsylvania statewide scope for this period. These are the complete returned set (no nextPageToken). This is sparse — it reflects that much Allegheny County material has not been digitized at the county level within FamilySearch's volume index.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company records, union records, immigration and industrial collections | In-person; contact for research services |
| Rivers of Steel archives (Homestead) | Steel-industry records, mill photographs, worker oral histories | In-person; contact for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories (1810s–), local history, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digital resources |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Marriage records, probate, deeds, court files, coroner records | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Land warrants/patents, factory inspector reports, state-level records | In-person; online request for some series |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Mid-Atlantic) | Federal naturalization records, passenger manifests for this region | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact for access |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records (Carnegie Steel, U.S. Steel, and other mill operators) — physical only at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel
- Union membership records (Amalgamated Association) — physical, fragmentary
- County coroner records for mill accidents — physical at Allegheny County courthouse
- Most Catholic ethnic parish registers for 1860–1900 — physical at parishes or Diocese of Pittsburgh
- County property tax assessment rolls — physical at courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives
- Allegheny City (pre-1907 annexation) municipal records — physical
- Pennsylvania factory inspector annual reports — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally in a 1921 fire and water damage event — no substitute exists for that census year. Use 1888–1892 city directories, state factory reports, and church records to bridge this gap.
- No courthouse fire of record for Allegheny County has been confirmed in the tool results — this county's records are generally intact, which is a relative advantage.

## Research tips
- **Identify the ethnic group before searching church records.** Pittsburgh's Catholic parishes were organized by national origin, not geography. A Slovak family in Homestead attended a Slovak parish; searching the Irish or German parish register will find nothing. Determine the immigrant's country of origin from the 1900 census (which lists birthplace of both parents) before going to church records. Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)
- **Use city directories as your intercensal tracker.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh directories from the 1810s onward. For the 1860–1900 window — especially the 1890 census gap — an annual directory entry showing name, occupation, and address is often the only annual-resolution evidence available. Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Search both Pittsburgh and Allegheny City records before 1907.** The north-bank city of Allegheny (now the North Side) was a separate municipality with its own courthouse and vital records until annexation in 1907. A family living across the river appears in Allegheny City records, not Pittsburgh's.
- **Check all three naturalization court series.** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court, other state courts, or federal courts. Search all three sets; a worker's Declaration of Intention and his Petition may be in different courts years apart.
- **The 1900 census is exceptionally rich for immigrant mill workers.** It records year of immigration, years in the US, and citizenship status — use it to frame the naturalization and passenger manifest search.
- **Don't skip the FamilySearch wiki page for Allegheny County.** The county's own genealogy page ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)) enumerates neighboring counties and specific local repositories not covered in the statewide pages.
- **Adjoining counties also hosted mill towns.** Homestead straddles the county line; Westmoreland, Washington, Beaver, and Butler counties each had their own mill communities. When a worker disappears from Allegheny County between censuses, check those counties' records.
- **The four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned only a generic 'Genealogy Research Guide' page** — the Pennsylvania-specific wiki pages did not load in this session. Consult the Pennsylvania Genealogy page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy for state-specific research strategies.

Philadelphia in 1793 was the capital of the United States and the largest city in the country, with roughly 50,000 residents. Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration at the time, so the deaths of approximately 5,000 people during the yellow fever epidemic from August through November 1793 were recorded almost entirely in **church burial registers** rather than government death certificates.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Cook County (Chicago), Illinois — Great Fire Context (ca. 1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1831 from unorganized territory
- **County seat:** Chicago
- **Economy:** Railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber trade, grain commerce, manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Bohemian, English, and native-born Americans
- **Key historical event:** The **Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871** — ~300 deaths, ~100,000 homeless, ~3.3 square miles destroyed. The Cook County Courthouse burned, taking deeds, birth/death registers, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers.

---

## The Fire as a Records Event

The destruction of the Cook County Courthouse is the **organizing fact** of every research problem here. Split every search at October 1871:

- **Before October 1871:** Use surviving federal records, pre-fire church registers from parishes outside the burn zone, and substitute sources (city directories, naturalization records).
- **After October 1871:** The new county record-keeping series begin and are more systematically available.

After the fire, Illinois passed the **Burnt Record Act of 1872**, requiring property owners to re-register deeds. The Chicago Title and Trust Company assembled insurance/title records that serve as partial substitutes for destroyed deed books — now held at the **Chicago History Museum**.

---

## Known Record Losses

| What Was Lost | When | Substitute |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-1871 Cook County deed books | Oct. 1871 | Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstruction; Chicago Title collection at Chicago History Museum |
| Pre-1871 birth & death registers | Oct. 1871 | Church registers, census mortality schedules, newspapers |
| Pre-1871 probate files | Oct. 1871 | Post-fire probate of same individuals |
| Pre-1871 court records | Oct. 1871 | Some naturalization records partly survive |
| Pre-1871 tax rolls | Oct. 1871 | No direct substitute |
| Church registers in the burn zone | Oct. 1871 | Check each parish individually — peripheral parishes often survived |
| 1890 federal census (nationwide) | 1921 | 1880/1900 censuses; 1890 veterans schedule; city directories |

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records
- **Pre-1871:** Virtually all destroyed. Use church registers, mortality schedules, newspaper notices.
- **Cook County local registration:** Begins **1871** (post-fire)
- **Illinois statewide registration:** Did **not** begin until **1916**
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records)
  - Death Records, 1871–1947 (980,000 records)
  - Marriage Records, 1871–1920 (620,000 records)

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch:** "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" — 285,000 records (pre- and post-fire)
- **Catholic registers:** Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives
- **Critical point:** Parishes on Chicago's periphery or whose records were stored off-site survived. Don't assume a parish's records are gone without checking.
- German-language and Latin registers are common — translation may be needed.

### Census Records
- **The 1870 federal census is the critical pre-fire snapshot** — survived because originals were held in Washington
- **1880 mortality schedule** captures deaths in the year preceding the census (valuable for 1879–1880 deaths)
- **1870 mortality schedule** covers the year of the fire's aftermath
- No Illinois state census equivalent for the 1871–1880 gap

### Disaster-Specific Records — Chicago Relief and Aid Society ⭐
**The most important record class unique to this disaster.** The Society administered relief to fire survivors and kept detailed case files: names, addresses, household composition, loss descriptions, and disbursements — a near-census-level snapshot of affected families in late 1871 and 1872.
- **Where held:** Chicago History Museum (in-person only; **not online**)
- For families who were homeless or displaced, this may be the **only surviving 1871 record naming all household members**.

### Naturalization Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations from Cook County Circuit and Superior Courts survive from the **1840s** — among the **most valuable pre-fire records for immigrant families**
- Provide birthplace, arrival information, and often family relationships

### Military Records
- Civil War records held outside Cook County — **unaffected by the fire**
- Service records and pension indexes on Ancestry and Fold3 (subscription); full pensions via NARA

### Land Records
- Federal land patents: BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) — free
- Pre-fire deeds largely destroyed; post-1872 reconstruction series at Cook County Recorder of Deeds
- Chicago Title collection at Chicago History Museum is the primary pre-fire property substitute

### City Directories
- Published from **1839** onward; survived the fire because copies were held widely
- Name heads of household, address, and occupation **annually** — fills gaps between censuses
- Held at the **Newberry Library**; some years digitized on Ancestry

### Newspapers
- **Chicago Tribune** (founded 1847) published extensive lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and property loss claims in October–November 1871
- Families used newspaper notices to locate separated relatives after the fire
- Digitized and full-text searchable on **Newspapers.com** (subscription)

### Cemetery Records
- **Rosehill Cemetery** (1859–) and **Graceland Cemetery** (1860–) were north of the burn zone — records survived
- Headstone photos and transcriptions on FindAGrave (free)

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records 1833–1925; vital records 1871+; 2 digitized volumes (1865–1880) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census; mortality schedules; passenger lists; vital records; some city directories | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Chicago Tribune 1847+; full-text searchable | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Civil War service records, pension files, draft registrations | Subscription |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| **FindAGrave.com** | Cemetery headstone photos | Free |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal census originals; military records | Free to search |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title/Trust insurance records (pre-fire property substitute); **Chicago Relief and Aid Society case files**; photographs | In-person; chicagohistory.org |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories (1839–); maps; manuscripts | In-person; newberry.org |
| **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** | Post-1871 Cook County court, probate, and deed records | In-person; neiu.edu |
| **Bernardin Archives (Archdiocese of Chicago)** | Catholic parish registers | By appointment |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago)** | Federal court/naturalization records | In-person |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 | In-person or certified copy request |
| **Illinois State Archives, Springfield** | Military records; state land patents | In-person or mail |

---

## Top Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — the last pre-fire household snapshot, fully intact.
2. **Search the Chicago Tribune (Newspapers.com) for October–November 1871** — lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and family-search notices.
3. **Contact the Chicago History Museum about the Relief and Aid Society case files** — this is the unique, irreplaceable disaster source for displaced families.
4. **Check whether the family's parish was in the burn zone** before concluding church records are lost. The Bernardin Archives can confirm which registers survive.
5. **Surviving pre-fire naturalization records** from the Cook County courts are among the best sources for immigrant family origins.
6. **Use city directories (Newberry Library) annually** between census years — they are the most reliable annual locator for Chicago families.
7. **Adjoining counties** (Lake, McHenry, Kane, DuPage, Will) may hold 1880 census entries for families who relocated after the fire.

---

The Great Fire creates one of the hardest records gaps in American genealogy, but the combination of intact federal records, the disaster-specific Relief Society files, surviving church registers, pre-fire naturalization records, and comprehensive newspaper coverage gives you a solid multi-source strategy to trace affected families.

---

# Locality Guide: Cook County (Chicago), Illinois — Great Fire Context (ca. 1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1831 from unorganized territory
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this place in this window, so no census-year figure is confirmed here. Chicago was one of the fastest-growing American cities — the 1870 federal census (the last pre-fire enumeration) is the best surviving snapshot.
- **Economy:** Railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber trade, grain commerce, manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy immigrant population — Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Bohemian, and smaller groups of English and native-born Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (the largest single body), Lutheran (multiple language-specific synods), Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and smaller immigrant congregations (e.g. Norwegian Lutheran, German Reformed)
- **Key historical event:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — approximately 300 deaths, ~100,000 left homeless, ~3.3 square miles destroyed. The Cook County Courthouse burned, taking with it deeds, birth and death registers, court records, probate files, tax rolls, and many church registers. This is the central fact shaping every research strategy for this place and period. ([Wikipedia: Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))

## Boundary changes

Cook County's boundaries were stable throughout this period. Chicago itself expanded by annexation in later decades but remained within Cook County. No boundary complication affects which county's records to search for the 1860–1890 window.

---

## The fire as a records event — what this means for research

The destruction of the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871 is not background color; it is the organizing fact of every research problem in this place. The records destroyed included:

- Pre-1871 deed books
- Pre-1871 birth and death registers held at the county level
- Pre-1871 probate files
- Pre-1871 court records (civil, criminal, naturalization)
- Pre-1871 tax rolls
- Many local church registers (parishes within the burn zone)

The 1870 federal census for Chicago **survived** because the originals were held in Washington, not in the courthouse. Federal records held outside Cook County survived generally.

After the fire, Illinois passed the **Burnt Record Act of 1872**, requiring property owners to re-register their deeds. This reconstruction effort created a new deed series starting in 1872. The Chicago Title and Trust Company (later Chicago Title) assembled insurance and title records that serve as partial substitutes for destroyed deed books; that collection is now at the **Chicago History Museum**. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))

The research strategy for any family in Chicago around 1871 must therefore split cleanly:
- **Before October 1871:** Use surviving federal records, pre-fire church registers from parishes outside the burn zone, and substitute sources (city directories, naturalization records in courts outside the courthouse).
- **After October 1871:** The new county record-keeping series begin. These are more systematically available.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date — county level:** Cook County birth and death records begin from **1871** (county level). This is the local series. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration))
- **Start date — statewide:** Illinois statewide vital registration did **not** begin until **1916**, with compliance improving through the 1920s. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration))
- **What exists on FamilySearch:**
  - Birth Certificates, 1871–1940 — 1,450,000 records (collection ID 2024189)
  - Death Records, 1871–1947 — 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)
  - Marriage Records, 1871–1920 — 620,000 records (collection ID 1756321)
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch has microfilmed post-fire records
- **Gaps:** Virtually all pre-October 1871 vital records at the county level were destroyed in the fire. Pre-fire births, marriages, and deaths must be reconstructed from church registers, census mortality schedules, and obituaries.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see below); 1870 federal census mortality schedule; newspaper death and marriage notices

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic, Lutheran (multiple German- and Scandinavian-language synods), Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Norwegian Lutheran, German Reformed, and others
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls
- **Critical point:** Many parish registers within the burn zone were destroyed. Parishes on the city's periphery or whose records were stored off-site survived. Do not assume a parish's records are gone without checking — some registers were salvaged.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978). Dates to 1833, covering both pre- and post-fire parish series.
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic registers: Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives
  - Lutheran, other Protestant: varies by synod; FamilySearch microfilm holds many
  - FamilySearch has digitized a significant portion (see collection above)
- **Language:** German-language registers are common for Lutheran and Catholic immigrant parishes; Latin is used in Catholic sacramental registers. The researcher must be able to read these or use a translator.
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed (the 285,000-record collection is indexed); individual parish volumes vary — some are browse-only images

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930 available. The **1870 census is the critical pre-fire snapshot** — it survived because the originals were held in Washington. The **1890 federal census was largely destroyed** nationwide (a separate disaster in 1921).
- **State census:** Illinois did not conduct a regular statewide census series equivalent to a federal enumeration in this period; no state census substitute fills the 1871–1880 gap.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1870 and 1880 federal mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding each census. These are available on FamilySearch and Ancestry and are especially valuable for identifying fire-related deaths in the 1870–1871 window.
- **Access:** 1870 and 1880 federal census — indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules — indexed on Ancestry; partially indexed on FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records

- **Pre-1871:** Probate files held in the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in the fire. Surviving fragments are rare.
- **Post-1871:** A new probate series begins. The Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County records from the post-1871 period.
- **Naturalization records:** Cook County naturalization records (Circuit Court and Superior Court) survive from the **1840s** for pre-fire naturalizations — these were court filings and at least some survived or were reconstructed. This is one of the most important surviving pre-fire record classes for immigrant families. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- **Digitization level:** Post-fire probate — microfilm at FamilySearch Library; some digitized volumes (see volume search below). Pre-fire naturalization fragments — physical and microfilm; check FamilySearch catalog.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office (original patents available via BLM GLO website, glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Largely destroyed. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 produced a new deed series. The Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum are the primary substitute for pre-fire property ownership.
- **Post-1872 deeds:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds holds the reconstructed and new series. IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University also holds county records.
- **Tax records:** Pre-1871 tax rolls destroyed; post-fire tax records begin anew.
- **Digitization level:** Post-fire deed and property re-recordings — FamilySearch has 2 digitized volumes for the 1865–1880 window (imageGroupNumbers 009982110 and 009982111; see below).

### Digitized volumes (FamilySearch)

Two digitized volumes were returned by `volume_search` for Cook County, 1860–1890:

| Volume | Image Group | Date range | Record type | Indexing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 009982110 | 1865–1871 | Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies) | 0% indexed — browse-only images |
| 2 | 009982111 | 1871–1880 | Post-fire Property Re-recordings | 41% name-indexed |

Volume 1 must be browsed image by image with no name search. Volume 2 is partially searchable by name. The total digitized volume count for this place and period is 2 — this is a coverage gap, not a complete digitization picture; consult FamilySearch catalog and IRAD for further holdings.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865). Many Chicago men served in Illinois infantry and cavalry regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations (Civil War draft records 1863–1865), bounty land warrants (pre-1855 service), regimental histories
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA), Washington D.C. and regional facilities; Illinois State Archives (state militia records); Fold3.com (Civil War service records and pension indexes, subscription)
- **Survival note:** Federal military records were held outside Cook County and were unaffected by the 1871 fire. These are fully intact.
- **Digitization level:** Civil War service records — indexed on Ancestry and Fold3 (subscription); pension indexes free on FamilySearch; full pension files require NARA request or Fold3 subscription.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Rosehill Cemetery (1859–, north of the burn zone, records survived), Graceland Cemetery (1860–), St. Boniface (German Catholic), Calvary Cemetery (Catholic, Evanston), and others
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com covers major Chicago cemeteries with reasonable completeness; some sexton records are online.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at the cemeteries themselves; some transferred to IRAD or historical societies. Rosehill and Graceland records survived the fire.
- **Digitization level:** Headstone photos — largely crowdsourced on FindAGrave (free); sexton/burial registers vary.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (founded 1847) and Chicago Times are the major survivors. The Tribune published extensive lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and property loss claims in October–November 1871. These are an irreplaceable primary source for identifying affected families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com and ProQuest Historical Newspapers (subscription) hold digitized Tribune issues. The Newberry Library holds microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, fire loss notices, relief recipient lists, "lost and found" notices posted after the fire (families separated during the evacuation used newspapers to locate each other)
- **Digitization level:** Chicago Tribune 1847 onward — digitized and full-text searchable on Newspapers.com (subscription); some issues on ProQuest.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland; immigrants typically arrived through New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island), Baltimore, New Orleans, or Quebec, then traveled inland by rail or lake steamer.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (held at NARA; searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch); naturalization declarations and petitions (Cook County courts, surviving from 1840s); alien registration; passport applications
- **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — Cook County Circuit Court, Superior Court, U.S. District Court. Surviving pre-fire naturalization records from the 1840s–1860s are among the most valuable pre-fire records for immigrant families. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))
- **Digitization level:** Passenger lists — indexed and searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch (free); pre-1906 Cook County naturalizations — partially microfilmed; check FamilySearch catalog.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax
- **Pre-1871:** Destroyed in the fire
- **Post-1871:** Cook County Assessor records; IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are especially important for the years between censuses (1871–1879) when no census and limited vital records exist.

### Disaster-specific records — the Chicago Relief and Aid Society

This is the single most important record class unique to the 1871 fire context. The Chicago Relief and Aid Society administered disaster relief to fire survivors and kept detailed case files on families who applied for assistance: names, addresses, household composition, loss descriptions, and disbursements. These records are a near-census-level snapshot of affected families in late 1871 and 1872.

- **Where held:** Chicago History Museum (the Society's records form part of their manuscript collections)
- **Access:** In-person research at the Chicago History Museum; some finding aid information online at chicagohistory.org
- **Content value:** For families who were homeless or displaced, this may be the only surviving 1871 record naming household members by name

### City directories

City directories for Chicago were published from **1839** onward and are held at the **Newberry Library**. They list heads of household, address, and occupation annually — filling the gaps between census years and providing pre-fire snapshots that survived the fire (directories were printed, distributed, and held in many locations). ([FamilySearch Wiki: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))

- **Digitization level:** Partial — some years are digitized on Ancestry (subscription); others require the Newberry Library in person or microfilm.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Cook County Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000); 2 digitized volumes (1865–1880) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census (1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910); mortality schedules; passenger lists; Cook County vital records (overlapping with FamilySearch); city directories (some years); Civil War service and pension indexes | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Civil War service records, pension files, draft registrations | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Chicago Tribune and Chicago Times (1847 onward); full-text searchable | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patent records for Illinois | Free |
| FindAGrave.com | Chicago cemetery headstone photos and transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal census originals, NARA-held naturalization records, military records | Free to search; fee for some record copies |

**Coverage note:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes for this place and period — that is the total matched set returned, not a paginated subset (no `nextPageToken` was present). This is a thin digitization footprint; the FamilySearch catalog and IRAD hold additional microfilmed material not reflected in these 2 volumes.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust insurance records (pre-fire property substitute); Chicago Relief and Aid Society case files; photographs; personal papers | In-person; chicagohistory.org for finding aids |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1839–); maps; manuscripts; genealogical collections | In-person; some digitized at newberry.org |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University | Post-1871 Cook County court, probate, and deed records | In-person; contact IRAD at neiu.edu |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | Military records; state land patents; state-level records | In-person or mail; ilsos.gov/departments/archives |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871; marriage licenses | In-person or certified copy request |
| Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | By appointment; search request submission online |
| National Archives — Great Lakes Region (Chicago) | Federal court records; naturalization records; federal agency records | In-person; archives.gov/chicago |

---

## Records NOT online

- Chicago Relief and Aid Society case files (1871–1873) — physical only at Chicago History Museum
- Chicago Title and Trust pre-fire insurance/title records — physical only at Chicago History Museum
- Most pre-1871 city directory runs beyond what Ancestry has digitized — Newberry Library only
- Post-1871 Cook County probate files (full case packets) — IRAD; microfilm at FamilySearch Library; not searchable online
- Catholic parish registers for many parishes — Bernardin Archives; some but not all are on FamilySearch microfilm
- IRAD deed and court records — physical and microfilm; not broadly digitized online

---

## Known record losses

| What was lost | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-1871 Cook County deed books | October 8–10, 1871 | Partial substitute: Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstruction series; Chicago Title collection at Chicago History Museum |
| Pre-1871 county-level birth and death registers | October 8–10, 1871 | Substitute: church registers, census mortality schedules, newspapers |
| Pre-1871 Cook County probate files | October 8–10, 1871 | No direct substitute; look for family mentions in post-fire probate of the same individuals |
| Pre-1871 Cook County court records (civil, criminal) | October 8–10, 1871 | Pre-fire naturalization records from Circuit and Superior courts partly survive |
| Pre-1871 tax rolls | October 8–10, 1871 | No direct substitute for pre-fire tax records |
| Many local church registers within the burn zone | October 8–10, 1871 | Check each parish individually; peripheral and suburban parishes often survived |
| 1890 federal census (nationwide) | 1921 fire at Commerce Dept. | Substitute: 1880 and 1900 censuses; 1890 veterans schedule (partially survived); city directories |

---

## Research tips

1. **Always start with the 1870 federal census** for anyone in Chicago before the fire. It is the last pre-fire population snapshot and survived because originals were in Washington. It establishes household composition, birthplace, age, and occupation just 12 months before the fire.

2. **Split every search at October 1871.** For a Cook County record type, ask first: does the pre-fire series survive? Usually the answer is no for county-held records. Then ask: does the post-fire series exist and where does it start?

3. **Illinois statewide vital registration did not begin until 1916 (state level); Cook County local registration begins at 1871 (county level).** A birth or death between 1860 and 1870 in Chicago has no surviving county register — go to church records first. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Illinois Vital Records — Statewide Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration))

4. **Surviving pre-fire naturalization records are among the most valuable sources for immigrant families.** Cook County Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s. These name birthplace, arrival information, and often family relationships. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records))

5. **Search the Chicago Tribune for October–November 1871.** The newspaper published lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and displaced persons. Families used the newspaper's "notices" columns to locate separated relatives. This is not indexed by name — it must be browsed — but it is digitized on Newspapers.com.

6. **The Chicago Relief and Aid Society records are unique to this disaster.** For families who were homeless or displaced after the fire, the Society's case files may be the only surviving 1871–1872 document naming all household members. These are at the Chicago History Museum and are not online.

7. **Church records outside the burn zone survived.** Parishes on Chicago's north and west periphery, and in suburban Cook County towns (Evanston, Hyde Park, Oak Park), were outside the fire's path. If you know or suspect where a family worshipped, check whether that parish was in the burn zone before concluding records are gone. The Archdiocese of Chicago's Bernardin Archives can confirm which registers survive for each parish.

8. **City directories (Newberry Library, 1839–)** are annual and name every head of household with address and occupation. They are the most reliable tool for locating a family in Chicago in any year between censuses, and they survived the fire because printed copies were held outside the burn zone. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire))

9. **Key repositories named directly in FamilySearch Wiki tool results:**
   - Newberry Library: city directories, maps, manuscripts
   - Chicago History Museum: insurance/title records, Relief Society files, photographs
   - IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University: post-1871 Cook County records
   - Bernardin Archives: Catholic parish registers
   - Cook County Clerk: vital records from 1871
   ([FamilySearch Wiki: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories))

10. **Adjoining counties:** Cook County borders Lake, McHenry, Kane, DuPage, and Will counties. Families who fled the fire often relocated temporarily to these counties. The 1880 census in those counties may pick up displaced households that do not appear in Chicago city directories. Neighboring county church records (especially German and Scandinavian Lutheran parishes) may hold transfers from burned Chicago parishes.

Chicago families around the Great Fire of 1871 present one of the most challenging record gaps in American genealogy because the courthouse fire wiped out almost everything the county held before that date. The good news is that federal records survived intact, church registers outside the burn zone were unaffected, naturalization records from the courts partly survived, and a remarkable disaster-specific source — the Chicago Relief and Aid Society case files at the Chicago History Museum — names thousands of affected households in a way no routine record would.

The next step is to anchor your specific ancestor in the 1870 federal census, check the 1871–1872 Chicago Tribune on Newspapers.com, and contact the Chicago History Museum about the Relief and Aid Society case files for that family.

---

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s, c. 1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Established:** French Louisiana was founded as a colonial territory in 1699; New Orleans was established in 1718 and became the administrative capital.
- **Administrative structure:** The colony was governed by a military governor with civil matters handled by the **Superior Council (Conseil Superieur)** — the chief governmental body for legal, land, and judicial records.
- **Ecclesiastical structure:** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana. Catholic parishes — not civil offices — held all vital records. The hierarchy ran: local parish → Diocese of Quebec (early) → Diocese of Louisiana and the Two Floridas.
- **Population:** Sparse frontier settlement.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Acadian exiles (from 1755 deportation), German Coast settlers, enslaved Africans and African descendants, Native nations. The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, making Catholic registers the record source for that population as well.
- **Key historical events:** 1699 — French settlement begins; 1718 — New Orleans founded; 1755 — Acadian deportees begin arriving; 1762 — Treaty of Fontainebleau cedes western Louisiana to Spain; 1769 — Spain takes effective administrative control.

---

## Boundary changes

The 1700s in Louisiana spans **two distinct colonial administrations**, each affecting where records were created and are now held:

- **French period: 1699–1762.** The entire territory from the Gulf Coast to the Illinois country was under French crown administration. The Superior Council in New Orleans created legal and land records for the whole colony.
- **Spanish period: 1762/1769–1800.** Spain took actual administrative control in 1769. Language of official records shifts from French to Spanish after 1769.

> **Research implication:** If you are researching the eastern bank of the Mississippi (which went to Britain in 1762, becoming British West Florida), those records are a separate jurisdiction entirely.

---

## Available record types

### Church records (most important category)

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons, required by the Code Noir), marriages (with pre-nuptial investigations and banns), burials, and confirmations.
- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans:** Sacramental registers survive from **1720**.
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection ID 1612905) — ~988,000 indexed records with images. This is the primary online access point. [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905]
- **Two browse-only volumes** on FamilySearch (DGS 004330991): Sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803, 264 images. **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish.** Must be browsed image-by-image.
- **Language:** French for the colonial period (Latin for some liturgical entries); Spanish after 1769.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in French colonial Louisiana.** The Catholic Church held all vital records. Civil registration came much later, after Louisiana became a U.S. state.

### Census records

- **Colonial census rolls:** French colonial administration took periodic enumerations. Held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France (partially digitized). No U.S. Federal Census exists for this period.

### Probate and court records

- **Superior Council records (1699–1769):** The Superior Council served as the court of record. Records include land grants, court proceedings, contracts, wills, and estate inventories.
  - Held at: **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans. Partially digitized.
