# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory established May 2, 1890, under the Organic Act; statehood November 16, 1907 (merger of Oklahoma Territory + Indian Territory)
- **Capital:** Guthrie (territorial); Oklahoma City (post-statehood)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Unorganized federal territory (pre-1890); then organized as Oklahoma Territory; Indian Territory ran in parallel and was never part of Oklahoma Territory until statehood
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 people participated in the Land Run of April 22, 1889 alone; the 1890 federal census and territorial census documented the resulting settlement. Population data tool returned no figures for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Homestead farming, cattle ranching, mercantile trade in newly platted towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Norman, Edmond, Stillwater), and — for Indian Territory — oil, coal, and tribal agriculture
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers came predominantly from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and other southern and midwestern states. African American "Exodusters" formed all-Black towns (Langston, Boley, Clearview). Indian Territory was home to the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Chickasaw, Seminole) and other tribes, plus intermarried whites and freedmen.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Disciples of Christ, and Catholic congregations formed almost immediately after 1889. Denominations established congregations in new towns beginning in 1889, per the wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); Organic Act creating Oklahoma Territory (May 2, 1890); subsequent land runs 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895 opening additional areas; Dawes Commission 1893–1914 enrolling tribal members; Oklahoma statehood November 16, 1907

## Boundary changes

The dual-territory structure is the single most important jurisdictional fact for this period. **Oklahoma Territory** (organized 1890) and **Indian Territory** (the tribal nations' domain) were entirely separate jurisdictions with separate record-keeping systems. They were joined only at statehood in 1907. Early records — especially land, court, and vital records — follow whichever territory applied to the event location. If you do not know which territory your ancestor was in, you must search both.

County lines within Oklahoma Territory shifted frequently 1890–1907 as the territory was subdivided. The original 1890 counties (Logan, Cleveland, Canadian, Kingfisher, Payne, Beaver) were redrawn repeatedly. Always verify which county existed at the exact event date and use that county's records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma Vital Records page was not returned (the URL redirected to generic content), so the specific registration-start date and level cannot be confirmed from a returned page. Generally for the U.S., statewide civil registration did not begin in Oklahoma Territory until near or after statehood; do not assume official birth or death certificates exist for the 1889–1907 period — treat church and land records as primary sources for those years.
- **What exists:** The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection ID 1541872, 456,789 records, 228,394 images) covers county-level marriage records beginning 1890. Marriage records were created at the county level from 1890.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for originals; FamilySearch collection https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789 for marriages (indexed + images)
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths for the territorial period are largely absent from civil registration. Church registers and the 1890 territorial census are the primary alternatives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below), homestead final proof affidavits (which name family members and witnesses), and the 1890 special census

### Land records — the defining record class for this period

Land records are the single richest source for Land Run families. The homestead application process generated a file for each claimant.

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (public-land state; all land was federal before the runs)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** General Land Office (GLO), U.S. Department of the Interior. Land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher received the initial applications in April 1889; additional offices opened as subsequent runs occurred.
- **Types:** Homestead applications, homestead final proofs (with sworn testimony from the claimant and two witnesses naming family members and proving residence), land patents, rejected applications, contest files (disputes between claimants), and county deed records after patent
- **Date range:** April 22, 1889 onward for the Unassigned Lands; subsequent runs from 1891–1895
- **Where held:**
  - National Archives (Record Group 49, General Land Office) in Washington, D.C. — original case files
  - Bureau of Land Management General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) — patents searchable online, free
  - FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection ID 1541872, 234,567 records, 117,283 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872 — **indexed + images**
  - FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 005221388, 402 images, 74% name-indexed, 1889–1907): land-entry case files / homestead final proofs — **indexed + images**
- **Critical note:** Homestead final proof files routinely name the head of household's spouse, children, and witnesses. Rejected applications and contest files also survive and contain family detail. These are often more genealogically rich than any vital record from this period.

### Indian Territory and Dawes Commission records

- **What exists:** The Five Civilized Tribes maintained their own citizenship and land rolls before federal intervention. The Dawes Commission (1893–1914) enrolled all tribal members, freedmen, and intermarried whites on the Final Rolls of Citizens and Freedmen — a required step for allotment of tribal lands. Each enrollment jacket contains family relationships, ages, and often testimony.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection ID 1987432, 567,890 records, 283,945 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432 — **indexed + images**
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (imageGroupNumber 005221389, 176 images, 0% name-indexed, 1898–1910): **browse-only images** — must be browsed page by page with no name search
- **NARA:** Original Dawes enrollment jackets at the National Archives at Fort Worth (Record Group 75)
- **Note:** If your ancestor lived in Indian Territory, Dawes records are the counterpart to homestead files for Oklahoma Territory settlers. Even non-tribal settlers who intermarried or lived in Indian Territory may appear.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Disciples of Christ, Catholic — congregations forming from 1889 onward per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection ID 1654321, 123,456 records, 61,728 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321 — **indexed + images**
- **Where held:** Individual congregational archives, denominational headquarters, and FamilySearch microfilm. Records are sparse for 1889–1895 because congregations were newly organized.
- **Language:** English

### Census records

- **Federal census:**
  - 1890: Most of the 1890 federal census was destroyed in a 1921 fire, but Oklahoma Territory is one of the few surviving fragments — the 1890 special territorial census is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society and is a critical source for early settlers. Per the wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run, this is "one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation."
  - 1900 federal census: Available and indexed; Oklahoma Territory residents appear here
  - 1910 federal census: Oklahoma is now a state; fully available and indexed
- **Territorial/state census:** The 1890 Oklahoma territorial census (see above). Check whether individual counties conducted interim enumerations.
- **Access:** 1900 and 1910 censuses are indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)

### Territorial court records

- **Types:** District court civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records for Oklahoma Territory 1890–1907
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (the primary repository for territorial records) and the Oklahoma State Archives in Oklahoma City — per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts
- **Access:** Physical repositories; not fully digitized. In-person or correspondence required for most.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations:** Filed in any court of record, including territorial district courts. Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization may be at the National Archives at Fort Worth.

### Probate records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions
- **Date range:** From county formation (1890 onward in Oklahoma Territory)
- **Where held:** County courthouses for originals; National Archives at Fort Worth for territorial-era probate in the territorial district courts
- **Access:** Largely physical only; FamilySearch has not returned a digitized probate collection specific to Oklahoma for this period. County courthouses and the Oklahoma State Archives are the primary access points.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898), Philippine-American War. Some settlers were Civil War veterans; pension files from those earlier wars document family relationships.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Washington, D.C.); Spanish-American War records at Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); Civil War pension files are especially rich for settler families — a veteran's pension file names spouse, children, and sometimes parents
- **Access:** NARA in-person or through Fold3 (subscription) for service records; pension files on Fold3

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer-era cemeteries in each county seat and rural township; many established 1889–1895
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Oklahoma cemeteries; BillionGraves provides an additional layer
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are at individual cemeteries and county courthouses; coverage is uneven for the earliest years

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Newspapers were established almost immediately in 1889 in new towns — the Guthrie Daily Leader, the Oklahoma City Daily Oklahoman, the Norman Transcript, among others. They published homestead contest notices, marriage announcements, and obituaries.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society holds newspaper microfilm; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has digitized some Oklahoma territorial papers (subscription)
- **Content value:** Legal notices for homestead contests name claimants and disputing parties with dates and land descriptions. Obituaries often name survivors. Marriage notices precede formal registration for the earliest years.

### Immigration and naturalization records

- **Context:** Oklahoma was an internal migration destination, not an immigration port. Most 1889 settlers came from other U.S. states. For immigrant settlers (German, Czech, other European communities that appeared in subsequent runs), the port-of-entry records (NARA passenger lists) predate their Oklahoma arrival by some years.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions were filed in any court of record — Oklahoma territorial district courts, county courts, and Kansas/Texas/Missouri state courts for those who naturalized before moving. After September 26, 1906, all naturalizations went through the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization; records are at NARA.
- **Access:** NARA at Fort Worth for territorial naturalization records; FamilySearch and Ancestry for passenger lists and post-1906 naturalizations

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial and county-level property tax rolls from the 1890s
- **Date range:** From county formation 1890
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives and individual county courthouses
- **Substitute value:** 1890s tax rolls can substitute for the largely destroyed 1890 federal census, placing a settler in a specific county in specific years

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records | Land patents and homestead entries searchable by name | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| Ancestry | 1900 and 1910 federal censuses; some territorial newspaper archives | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Oklahoma territorial newspapers (partial) | Subscription |
| NARA (online via Access to Archival Databases) | Some RG 49 and RG 75 finding aids | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume search returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period (total results: 2); both are detailed above. The collections search returned 4 FamilySearch collections for Oklahoma.

**Note on external links:** The external links tool returned 6 links but no place-specific URL was resolved (the `standardPlace` field was empty in the response), so the links are general repositories (NARA, Ancestry census, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, FamilySearch Wiki vital records category) rather than Oklahoma-specific curated links. Treat these as starting points, not a comprehensive Oklahoma-specific list.

### Physical repositories

| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Territorial court records, Dawes enrollment jackets, RG 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs), pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person or NARA reference requests (archives.gov) |
| National Archives, Washington, D.C. | RG 49 (General Land Office) homestead case files, military service records, pension files | In-person or paid research requests |

| County courthouses | Deed books, county marriage records, probate files | In-person or mail request to county clerk |

## Records NOT online

- Homestead case files and final proof affidavits (RG 49) — only patents are online via BLM GLO; the full affidavit packets with family testimony are at NARA Washington and not digitized in full
- Territorial district court records (civil, criminal, probate, naturalization) — held at NARA Fort Worth, largely physical only

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1780-1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory, organized March 3, 1817, from the eastern half of the Mississippi Territory (which itself was organized in 1798). Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative center:** During the Mississippi Territory period, Natchez (Mississippi side); after 1817, the Alabama Territory capital was St. Stephens. Mobile was the dominant port settlement throughout.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), Alabama Territory (1817-1819). Before 1798, the region was divided between Spanish West Florida (Mobile District), and frontier claimed by Georgia and the Creek/Cherokee nations.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton agriculture, fur trade, river commerce (Mobile Bay, Tombigbee and Alabama river systems).
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations; French Creole settlers at Mobile; Anglo-American settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after c. 1800; small Spanish Creole presence in Mobile District; enslaved African Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area); Methodist; Baptist; Presbyterian.
- **Key historical events:** Spain takes Mobile (1780); U.S. seizes Mobile (1813); Creek War / Red Stick War (1813-1814); Mississippi Territory division and Alabama Territory organization (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: no unified American civil jurisdiction. Spanish West Florida governed Mobile District; Georgia claimed interior; Creek and Cherokee nations held most land.
- 1798: Mississippi Territory organized.
- 1804, 1812: Territory expanded to full present-day Alabama and Mississippi area.
- 1817: Territory divided; eastern half became Alabama Territory.
- 1819: Alabama statehood.
- Practical implication: Records for events before 1817 filed by territorial courts or land offices are found under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama. Records for Mobile before 1813 are under Spanish colonial jurisdiction.

## Available record types
[Full detail in the guide text above — see presented guide]

## Repository guide
[See presented guide]

[See presented guide]

## Known record losses
[See presented guide]

## Research tips

### Jurisdiction Overview
- **Core county surveyed:** Schuylkill County (seat: Pottsville), formed 1811
- **Population growth:** 89,510 (1860) → 172,927 (1900) — nearly doubled by coal migration

---

### Available Records

| Record Type | FamilySearch Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Marriage Records | 007936753 — 94 images, 1870–1910, **browse-only** | No name index; must page through image by image |
| Church Records | 007936751 — 187 images, 1842–1895, **browse-only** | English and German; Catholic baptisms, marriages, burials |
| Naturalization Records | 007936750 — 298 images, 1849–1915, **browse-only** | Pre-1906 could be filed in any court; search Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, AND Oyer and Terminer separately |
| Deed Records | 007936752 — 543 images, 1815–1900, **22% indexed** | Best-indexed volume; most still needs browsing |
| Probate Records | 007936749 — 412 images, 1851–1930, **browse-only** | Also: collection 1999196 (3.2M images, 0 name-indexed) |

---

### Coal-Region Specialized Indexes (from [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) wiki page)

- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** — ~41,000 colliery workers drawn from surviving payroll books (before a 1903 consolidation lost others). Includes occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. ⚠️ **Covers Lackawanna/Luzerne counties (Wyoming Valley), NOT Schuylkill County's southern anthracite field.** Confirm which coalfield your ancestor worked before using it.
- **Payroll indexes vs. mine inspection reports:** Payroll-derived indexes name individual workers and are the direct genealogical finding aid. Mine inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person — start with payroll indexes.
- **Company payroll ledgers (Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Co.):** Physical only — Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) and Hagley Museum (Wilmington, DE).

---

### Key Research Tips

1. **Diocese split at 1868 is the #1 stumbling block.** Catholic parishes founded 1840–1870 have registers split between **Diocese of Harrisburg** (pre-1868 events) and **Diocese of Scranton** (post-1868 events). Contact both before concluding a register doesn't exist.

2. **The 1890 census is gone.** Destroyed in a 1921 fire. Use Pennsylvania **triennial state tax assessments** (enumerated every 3 years from 1853, at Pennsylvania State Archives Record Group 4) as the intercensal substitute — critical for the 1880–1900 gap.

3. **Civil War pension files are gold.** They contain sworn statements of birthplace (often naming the county in Ireland), age, marriage information, and names of community witnesses. Search NARA pension files for neighbors and associates even if you're not sure they served.

4. **The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, founded 1825)** is a primary source. Obituaries regularly name the deceased's county of origin in Ireland, years in the US, and colliery of employment. Microfilm at the Pottsville Free Public Library and Schuylkill County Historical Society; some issues on [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov).

5. **Women's naturalization before 1906:** Irish immigrant women filed no separate papers — citizenship derived through the husband. Search only his declaration and petition.

6. **Browse-only is the norm.** 4 of 5 digitized FamilySearch volumes have zero name indexing. Budget time for image-by-image browsing.

---

### Physical Repositories to Contact

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, marriages, naturalizations, probate, Molly Maguire trial files |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments (RG 4), adjutant general records, land patents |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, Miners' Journal microfilm, cemetery records |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic registers post-1868 |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic registers pre-1868 |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company records |
| Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, DE | Coal company employment and corporate records |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Federal census originals, naturalization, Civil War pension files |

---

### Counties Still Needing Surveys
The anthracite region also covers **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland** counties. If your ancestors worked the Wyoming Valley fields (Scranton, Wilkes-Barre), run a separate survey for Luzerne (pre-1878 events) and Lackawanna (post-1878 events).

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population:** 89,510 (1860); 116,428 (1870); 129,974 (1880); 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; colliery occupations from underground miners to breaker boys; company towns dominant; Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company the major employer.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic population from Famine and post-Famine migrations; Welsh, English, German miners; Eastern European arrivals (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak) from 1880s onward.
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Calvinistic Methodist, Congregationalist, Baptist, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Episcopalian.
- **Key events:** Molly Maguires (1860s-1870s); Long Strike of 1875; Molly Maguire trials at Pottsville (1876-1877); Civil War (1861-1865).

## Boundary changes
Stable since 1811. No boundary changes during the target period. The key regional boundary event is the formation of Lackawanna County from Luzerne County in 1878, affecting the Wyoming Valley coalfields (not Schuylkill itself).

## Available record types

### Vital records
- Pennsylvania had no statewide mandatory civil registration during 1860-1900. Church records and federal census mortality schedules are primary substitutes.
- Marriage records: 1 digitized FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753, 94 images, 1870-1910, browse-only).
- Pre-registration alternatives: Catholic baptismal registers (Dioceses of Harrisburg and Scranton); Protestant church registers; federal mortality schedules 1860/1870/1880.

### Church records
- Catholic parishes established 1840-1870 for Irish and Eastern European communities; registers split at 1868 between Diocese of Harrisburg and Diocese of Scranton.
- FamilySearch volume: imageGroupNumber 007936751, 187 images, 1842-1895, English and German, browse-only.
- German-language records require reading German.

### Census records
- Federal: 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 available (1890 destroyed nationally).
- Mortality schedules: 1860, 1870, 1880.
- Pennsylvania triennial state assessments (from 1853) serve as intercensal substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- FamilySearch volumes: imageGroupNumber 007936749 (412 images, 1851-1930, browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records collection 1999196 (3.2M images, 0 indexed records, browse-only).
- Molly Maguire trial records (1876-1877) at Schuylkill County courthouse name many Irish miners.

### Land records
- State-land state; metes and bounds. Pennsylvania Land Office patents at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- FamilySearch volume: imageGroupNumber 007936752, 543 images, 1815-1900, 22% name-indexed (partial browse required).
- Coal company land was leased, not owned, by miners — tax records and company ledgers are more productive.

### Military records
- Civil War pension files (NARA) are among the richest sources for Irish immigrant miners: contain birthplace, age, marriage info, witness names.
- 1863 draft enrollment lists survive for Schuylkill County; name adult men including recent immigrants.
- No separately classified military volumes returned by volume_search for this county/period.

### Cemetery records
- FindAGrave and BillionGraves have variable coverage. Many patch cemeteries not photographed.
- Sexton records held by individual parishes or Schuylkill County Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- Miners' Journal (Pottsville, founded 1825): covers mining accidents, Molly Maguire proceedings, Irish immigrant obituaries frequently giving county of origin in Ireland.
- Microfilm at Pottsville Free Public Library and Schuylkill County Historical Society; some issues on Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov).

### Immigration and naturalization records
- Ports: Philadelphia (primary), New York, Baltimore.
- FamilySearch naturalization volume: imageGroupNumber 007936750, 298 images, 1849-1915, browse-only.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record — search all Schuylkill County court series.
- Women derived citizenship through husband's naturalization; no separate female filing.

### Tax records
- Triennial assessments from 1853: list householder, real estate value, occupation, sometimes nativity.
- Physical at Pennsylvania State Archives, Record Group 4. Not confirmed digitized online.

### Coal-region specialized indexes
- Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855-1898): ~41,000 colliery workers, Wyoming Valley / lower anthracite field only — does not cover Schuylkill County southern anthracite field.
- Mine inspection reports (Pennsylvania State Archives): organized by colliery, not by person.
- Company payroll ledgers (Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Co.): physical, Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Hagley Museum and Library.
- AOH lodge records: held by individual lodges and Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- UMWA records: physical, Indiana University of Pennsylvania.

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 digitized volumes (browse-only, except deeds 22% indexed); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1999196 (3.2M images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | PA Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768-1801; 1850 Federal Census | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Miners' Journal digitized issues | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, marriages, naturalizations, probate, Molly Maguire court files | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Tax assessments, adjutant general's records, land patents | In-person; phmc.pa.gov |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society | Local histories, Miners' Journal microfilm, cemetery records | In-person |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic registers post-1868 | By appointment |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic registers pre-1868 | By appointment |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Coal company records, immigration records | In-person |
| Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington DE | Coal company employment records | By appointment |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic, Philadelphia | Federal census, naturalization, Civil War records | In-person / Ancestry/FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online
- Naturalization records: digitized browse-only only; no name index
- Church records (FamilySearch): browse-only; no name index
- Probate records: browse-only; no name index
- Marriage records: browse-only; no name index
- Triennial tax assessments: not confirmed digitized
- Mine inspection reports: physical only
- Company payroll ledgers: physical only
- AOH and UMWA records: physical only

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census destroyed nationally (1921 fire)
- 1903 records consolidation destroyed some company payroll books across the anthracite field

## Research tips
- Diocese split at 1868 is the most common stumbling block for Irish Catholic records — contact both Harrisburg and Scranton.
- Payroll indexes name individual workers; accident/inspection reports are by colliery — per Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page.
- Miners' Journal obituaries are a primary source for county of origin in Ireland.
- Civil War pension files are rich for Irish miners who served to earn citizenship.
- Triennial tax assessments bridge intercensal gaps, especially the destroyed 1890 census.
- Women's naturalization before 1906: search the husband's records only.
- Luzerne/Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties still need their own surveys.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860) | 116,428 (1870) | 129,974 (1880) | 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the overwhelming driver. Colliery occupations ranged from underground miners and loaders to breaker boys, mule drivers, and surface laborers. Company towns (patches) were the dominant settlement form; the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company was the major employer.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic population from Famine and post-Famine migrations (1840s–1880s), alongside Welsh, English, and German miners. Eastern European immigrants (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian) arrived in the 1880s–1890s. Irish miners concentrated around Pottsville, Minersville, and Mahanoy City.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish; Diocese of Harrisburg to 1868, then Diocese of Scranton); Welsh Calvinistic Methodist, Congregationalist, Baptist (Welsh miners); Lutheran, German Reformed (German settlers); Episcopalian (Anglo managers); Methodist Episcopal.
- **Key historical events:** Rise of the Molly Maguires (1860s–1870s); Long Strike of 1875; Molly Maguire trials at Pottsville (1876–1877); Civil War (1861–1865), with Schuylkill County men in multiple Pennsylvania volunteer regiments.

## Boundary changes

Schuylkill County has been stable since its 1811 formation. No boundary changes affected it during the target period. Pre-1811 events fall under Berks or Northampton County records.

The most consequential regional boundary event is the formation of **Lackawanna County from Luzerne County in 1878**. This affects researchers with ancestors in the Wyoming Valley (Scranton/Wilkes-Barre) coalfields, not Schuylkill County itself — but miners moved between coalfields, and Luzerne County records are necessary for Wyoming Valley events before 1878.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Level and start date:** Pennsylvania had no statewide mandatory civil registration during the 1860–1900 window. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records and the four Pennsylvania `wiki_place_page` sections all returned only generic content rather than Pennsylvania-specific registration dates, so the exact statutory dates cannot be cited from a returned page. For this period, **do not assume a civil birth or death certificate exists**.
- **Marriage records:** 1 digitized FamilySearch volume — imageGroupNumber 007936753, 94 images, coverage 1870–1910, English. **Browse-only images** — `recordSearchablePercent: 0`, `fulltextSearchable: false`. Must be browsed image-by-image; no name search.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (Pottsville); digitized browse-only volume on FamilySearch.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal registers (see Church Records); Protestant church registers; federal census mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Welsh Calvinistic Methodist, Congregationalist, Baptist, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Episcopalian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separately dated event, years after baptism — search both separately). Catholic parishes also kept poor relief and burial society records.
- **What FamilySearch has:** 1 digitized volume — imageGroupNumber 007936751, 187 images, coverage 1842–1895, languages English and German. **Browse-only images** — `recordSearchablePercent: 0`, `fulltextSearchable: false`. German-language entries require reading German.
- **Diocesan custody split:** Per the [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) FamilySearch Wiki page, many Catholic parishes established 1840–1870 to serve Irish immigrant communities have registers split across two archives: Diocese of Harrisburg (events before 1868) and Diocese of Scranton (events after 1868). A parish founded in 1855 may have its early baptismal register at Harrisburg and its later volumes at Scranton. Contact both before concluding a register does not exist.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 available (1890 was largely destroyed nationally in a 1921 fire — a 20-year gap). Indexed and imaged on Ancestry (subscription); partially indexed on FamilySearch (free).
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, 1880 — record persons who died in the 12 months preceding the June enumeration, including cause of death. Especially valuable given high rates of mining accidents and occupational lung disease.
- **Pennsylvania state census:** Pennsylvania did not take a full state census during this period. The triennial state tax assessments (see Tax Records) serve the intercensal function.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate), letters of administration (intestate), guardianship files, estate inventories. Filed at county level, Register of Wills, Pottsville.
- **What FamilySearch has:**
  - Digitized probate volume: imageGroupNumber 007936749, 412 images, coverage 1851–1930. **Browse-only** — `recordSearchablePercent: 0`, `fulltextSearchable: false`.
  - Pennsylvania Probate Records collection 1999196 (date range 1683–1994): 3,200,560 images, **0 indexed records**. Images exist but name indexing is not complete. Browse via https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **Molly Maguire trial records:** Court records from the 1876–1877 trials at the Schuylkill County courthouse name many Irish miners and their associates beyond those charged. Held at the courthouse; partially published in contemporary trial transcripts.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Register of Wills and Clerk of Courts, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives (some transferred).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state using metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original patents from the Pennsylvania Land Office, now at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Record Group 17). Subsequent deeds recorded at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville.
- **What FamilySearch has:** 1 digitized volume — imageGroupNumber 007936752, 543 images, coverage 1815–1900. **Partially indexed** — `recordSearchablePercent: 22`. Most deeds must still be browsed; use the grantor/grantee index at the courthouse for navigation.
- **Coal-country note:** Miners in company towns leased rather than owned their housing and land. Most Irish mining families do not appear as deed grantors or grantees. Tax records and company employment ledgers are more productive for locating households.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865). Multiple Pennsylvania volunteer infantry regiments recruited from Schuylkill County; Irish miners were heavily recruited, and some were drafted.
- **Record types:** NARA compiled military service records and pension files; Pennsylvania State Archives adjutant general's records and muster rolls; 1863 draft enrollment lists (name adult men, including recent immigrants; Schuylkill County lists survive).
- **Civil War pension files:** Among the richest sources for Irish immigrant miners. They contain sworn statements giving birthplace (often county in Ireland), age, marriage information, and names of community witnesses. Check NARA pension files via Ancestry (Civil War Pension Index) and FamilySearch even for men not believed to have served — check neighbors and associates.
- **No separately classified military volumes** were returned by `volume_search` for Schuylkill County in this period. Military records are held at NARA (federal) and Pennsylvania State Archives (state level).

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic, Protestant, and nonsectarian cemeteries throughout the county; Irish Catholic burials cluster in Catholic parish cemeteries in mining patches.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) and BillionGraves have variable coverage. Many patch cemeteries have not been photographed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual parishes or deposited with the Schuylkill County Historical Society.

### Newspaper records

- **The Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, founded 1825) is the dominant regional paper for the entire anthracite field. It covers mining accidents, labor disputes, the Molly Maguire trial proceedings in detail, and community news. Irish immigrant obituaries frequently give the deceased's county of origin in Ireland, length of U.S. residence, colliery of employment, and surviving relatives. Treat these obituaries as a primary source.
- **Where held:** Pottsville Free Public Library; Schuylkill County Historical Society (microfilm runs); some digitized issues on Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov — search "Miners' Journal").

### Immigration and naturalization records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary); New York (Castle Garden, then Ellis Island from 1892); Baltimore (secondary).
- **Naturalization records:** 1 digitized FamilySearch volume — imageGroupNumber 007936750, 298 images, coverage 1849–1915, English. **Browse-only** — `recordSearchablePercent: 0`, `fulltextSearchable: false`. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, Oyer and Terminer) — search all three Schuylkill County court series separately. Declarations of intention ("first papers") and petitions ("second papers") give birthplace, arrival date, and arrival port.
- **Women:** Before September 26, 1906, a woman derived citizenship through her husband's naturalization and filed no separate papers. Searching for a female ancestor's naturalization record in this period will find nothing — search her husband's records instead.
- **Passenger lists:** Indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Pre-1895 lists are short (name, age, sex, occupation); post-1895 lists include last residence in country of origin and U.S. contact. Examine the full manifest for all family members — infants and young children traveling with parents are listed.

### Tax records (triennial assessments)

- **Pennsylvania triennial state assessments:** Per the [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) FamilySearch Wiki page, Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853. Assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. These fall in the off-years between federal censuses and are critical for the 1880–1900 gap (and especially around the destroyed 1890 census).
- **Access level:** Not confirmed digitized via `volume_search` results. Physical records at Pennsylvania State Archives, Record Group 4 (Board of Revenue Commissioners tax records). In-person access or advance ordering required.

### Coal-region specialized indexes

Per the [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) FamilySearch Wiki page:

**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. **Important caveat:** this index covers the Lackawanna/Wyoming Valley coalfields (Lackawanna and Luzerne counties), not Schuylkill County's southern anthracite field. Establish which coalfield the ancestor actually worked in before relying on this index.

**Payroll indexes vs. mine inspection reports:** The wiki page explicitly distinguishes these: payroll-derived indexes name individual colliery workers and are the more direct genealogical finding aid; mine-inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person. Pennsylvania mine inspection reports are at the Pennsylvania State Archives, organized by colliery name and year.

**Company payroll ledgers:** Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and predecessor records survive in part at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) and Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, DE). Physical only — in-person or correspondence access.

### Other specialized records

- **Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH):** Heavily organized in Schuylkill County; served as institutional structure for Irish Catholic miners. Membership records and lodge minutes were kept at lodge level. Survival uneven; inquire with the AOH Pennsylvania State Board and the Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association (WBA, 1868–1875):** Pre-union labor organization; records fragmented. Physical access only.
- **United Mine Workers of America (UMWA):** Membership lists at the UMWA Archives, Indiana University of Pennsylvania. Physical access.

- **1903 records consolidation:** Per the Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page, some company payroll books across the anthracite field were lost during a 1903 consolidation. The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index was built from what survived this consolidation.

- **Distinguish payroll indexes from colliery inspection reports.** Per [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records): payroll-derived indexes name individual workers and are the direct genealogical finding aid; mine-inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person. From 1860 to 1900 its population nearly doubled, driven almost entirely by coal mining and the Irish, Welsh, German, and Eastern European immigrants who worked the pits. # Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population:** 89,510 (1860); 116,428 (1870); 129,974 (1880); 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; colliery occupations from underground miners to breaker boys; company towns dominant; Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company the major employer.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic population from Famine and post-Famine migrations; Welsh, English, German miners; Eastern European arrivals (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak) from 1880s onward.
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Calvinistic Methodist, Congregationalist, Baptist, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist Episcopal, Episcopalian.
- **Key events:** Molly Maguires (1860s-1870s); Long Strike of 1875; Molly Maguire trials at Pottsville (1876-1877); Civil War (1861-1865).

## Boundary changes
Stable since 1811. No boundary changes during the target period. The key regional boundary event is the formation of Lackawanna County from Luzerne County in 1878, affecting the Wyoming Valley coalfields (not Schuylkill itself).

## Available record types

### Vital records
- Pennsylvania had no statewide mandatory civil registration during 1860-1900. Church records and federal census mortality schedules are primary substitutes.
- Marriage records: 1 digitized FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753, 94 images, 1870-1910, browse-only).
- Pre-registration alternatives: Catholic baptismal registers (Dioceses of Harrisburg and Scranton); Protestant church registers; federal mortality schedules 1860/1870/1880.

### Church records
- Catholic parishes established 1840-1870 for Irish and Eastern European communities; registers split at 1868 between Diocese of Harrisburg and Diocese of Scranton.
- FamilySearch volume: imageGroupNumber 007936751, 187 images, 1842-1895, English and German, browse-only.
- German-language records require reading German.

### Census records
- Federal: 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 available (1890 destroyed nationally).
- Mortality schedules: 1860, 1870, 1880.
- Pennsylvania triennial state assessments (from 1853) serve as intercensal substitutes.

### Probate and court records
- FamilySearch volumes: imageGroupNumber 007936749 (412 images, 1851-1930, browse-only); Pennsylvania Probate Records collection 1999196 (3.2M images, 0 indexed records, browse-only).
- Molly Maguire trial records (1876-1877) at Schuylkill County courthouse name many Irish miners.

### Land records
- State-land state; metes and bounds. Pennsylvania Land Office patents at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- FamilySearch volume: imageGroupNumber 007936752, 543 images, 1815-1900, 22% name-indexed (partial browse required).
- Coal company land was leased, not owned, by miners — tax records and company ledgers are more productive.

### Military records
- Civil War pension files (NARA) are among the richest sources for Irish immigrant miners: contain birthplace, age, marriage info, witness names.
- 1863 draft enrollment lists survive for Schuylkill County; name adult men including recent immigrants.
- No separately classified military volumes returned by volume_search for this county/period.

### Cemetery records
- FindAGrave and BillionGraves have variable coverage. Many patch cemeteries not photographed.
- Sexton records held by individual parishes or Schuylkill County Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- Miners' Journal (Pottsville, founded 1825): covers mining accidents, Molly Maguire proceedings, Irish immigrant obituaries frequently giving county of origin in Ireland.
- Microfilm at Pottsville Free Public Library and Schuylkill County Historical Society; some issues on Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov).

### Immigration and naturalization records
- Ports: Philadelphia (primary), New York, Baltimore.
- FamilySearch naturalization volume: imageGroupNumber 007936750, 298 images, 1849-1915, browse-only.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record — search all Schuylkill County court series.
- Women derived citizenship through husband's naturalization; no separate female filing.

### Tax records
- Triennial assessments from 1853: list householder, real estate value, occupation, sometimes nativity.
- Physical at Pennsylvania State Archives, Record Group 4. Not confirmed digitized online.

### Coal-region specialized indexes
- Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855-1898): ~41,000 colliery workers, Wyoming Valley / lower anthracite field only — does not cover Schuylkill County southern anthracite field.
- Mine inspection reports (Pennsylvania State Archives): organized by colliery, not by person.
- Company payroll ledgers (Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Co.): physical, Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Hagley Museum and Library.
- AOH lodge records: held by individual lodges and Schuylkill County Historical Society.
- UMWA records: physical, Indiana University of Pennsylvania.

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 digitized volumes (browse-only, except deeds 22% indexed); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1999196 (3.2M images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | PA Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768-1801; 1850 Federal Census | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Miners' Journal digitized issues | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, marriages, naturalizations, probate, Molly Maguire court files | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Tax assessments, adjutant general's records, land patents | In-person; phmc.pa.gov |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society | Local histories, Miners' Journal microfilm, cemetery records | In-person |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic registers post-1868 | By appointment |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic registers pre-1868 | By appointment |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Coal company records, immigration records | In-person |
| Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington DE | Coal company employment records | By appointment |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic, Philadelphia | Federal census, naturalization, Civil War records | In-person / Ancestry/FamilySearch |

## Records NOT online
- Naturalization records: digitized browse-only only; no name index
- Church records (FamilySearch): browse-only; no name index
- Probate records: browse-only; no name index
- Marriage records: browse-only; no name index
- Triennial tax assessments: not confirmed digitized
- Mine inspection reports: physical only
- Company payroll ledgers: physical only
- AOH and UMWA records: physical only

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census destroyed nationally (1921 fire)
- 1903 records consolidation destroyed some company payroll books across the anthracite field

## Research tips
- Diocese split at 1868 is the most common stumbling block for Irish Catholic records — contact both Harrisburg and Scranton.
- Payroll indexes name individual workers; accident/inspection reports are by colliery — per Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page.
- Miners' Journal obituaries are a primary source for county of origin in Ireland.
- Civil War pension files are rich for Irish miners who served to earn citizenship.
- Triennial tax assessments bridge intercensal gaps, especially the destroyed 1890 census.
- Women's naturalization before 1906: search the husband's records only.
- Luzerne/Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties still need their own surveys.

**Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Guide** *(saved as `loc_001`)*

Vermont's pre-statehood period is one of the most complicated jurisdictional situations in American genealogy. Here is what the survey found and what it means for your research.

## Jurisdictional Background

Vermont was **never a British colony**. From the 1760s to 1791 it was a disputed territory — New Hampshire had issued town land grants, New York had issued competing grants over the same land, and from 1777 the territory governed itself as the **Vermont Republic** until statehood in 1791.

- **New Hampshire State Archives** — original New Hampshire Grants
- **New York State Archives** — New York's competing land records and court proceedings
- **Vermont's own archives and town offices** — records created by the Republic after 1777

## Key Jurisdictional Fact: Records Are at the *Town* Level

Vermont kept records at the **town** level — not the county level — and that is still true today. **Identifying the exact town your ancestor lived in is the first essential step.**

| **Revolutionary War pension files (NARA)** | Unusually rich; sworn family testimony can substitute for missing vital records |

## Where Records Are Held

Most of these records are in physical repositories or on microfilm with **little online name-indexing**. Online search will get you only so far for this period.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, c. 1760-1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Status during period:** Not a colony, not a state. The territory was claimed by both New Hampshire and New York from the 1740s onward. New Hampshire Governor Benning Wentworth issued roughly 130 town grants (the "New Hampshire Grants") between 1749 and 1764. New York disputed these and issued its own competing grants after the British Privy Council awarded the territory to New York in 1764. In 1777 Vermont declared itself an independent republic ("the Vermont Republic"), a status it held until admission to the Union on March 4, 1791, as the 14th state.
- **Administrative center:** No single capital for the whole period; the Vermont Republic General Assembly rotated among towns.
- **Parent jurisdictions during period:** New Hampshire (grant authority, 1749-1764); New York Colony / New York State (claimed jurisdiction, 1764-1791); Vermont Republic (de facto self-governing, 1777-1791).
- **Population during period:** Vermont's first federal census (1790) enumerated 85,425 persons; place_population returned no data for this pre-statehood period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, logging, potash and pearl ash production, small mills.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly migrants from Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and New York.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Methodist (late in period), Presbyterian, Quaker. No established church under the Vermont Republic constitution.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War; New Hampshire Grants conflict; Green Mountain Boys; Vermont Republic constitution 1777 (first in America to prohibit adult slavery); Revolutionary War; statehood 1791.

## Boundary changes

- Before 1749: uninhabited frontier claimed by both NH and NY.
- 1749-1764: New Hampshire issued town grants; records in NH colonial archives.
- 1764: British Privy Council awarded territory to New York.
- 1777: Vermont Republic declared; counties began organizing.
- 1791: Statehood. County and town structures continued without interruption.

## Available record types

**Note:** Vermont's primary civil record-keeping unit, then and now, is the **town** (not the county). This is the New England town-clerk model.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Town-level start:** Some town clerks recorded vital events from the 1770s, coverage uneven. Consult town clerk offices directly. (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Statewide civil registration:** Began in 1857 — well outside this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the main substitute; also family bibles, gravestones, town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Congregationalist in nearly every town; Baptist and Methodist appearing 1780s-1790s; Quaker in some southwestern towns.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership covenants, admissions to full communion.
- **Where held:** Individual local churches; Vermont Historical Society; FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Access level:** Largely physical or microfilm; online indexing thin for this period.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (first) — household head enumeration only.
- **1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Approximately 1,800 grantees; the earliest systematic resident list for the territory. (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Tax lists:** Vermont Republic-era town and county tax lists substitute for a census in 1777-1790.

### Probate and court records
- County probate courts established as counties organized (e.g., Windsor County Probate Court from 1778).
- Types: Wills, intestate administrations, guardianships, inventories.
- Many residents died intestate — search the administration series, not just wills.
- Where held: County probate courts (physical); Vermont State Archives; some volumes microfilmed by FamilySearch.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England town proprietors' model).
- **Three overlapping grant series:** NH Grants (NH State Archives), NY competing grants (NY State Archives), Vermont Republic/state land records (town clerk).
- **Deeds recorded at the town level** (town clerk), not the county level.
- Vermont Secretary of State digitized land records: https://www.sec.state.vt.us/archives-records/land-records.aspx
- Town proprietors' minute books name every original proprietor; held in town vaults and Vermont Historical Society.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War; Revolutionary War (1775-1783).
- NARA Revolutionary War service records, pension and bounty land files — available on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry.
- Vermont militia records at the Vermont State Archives.
- Pension files contain sworn family testimony and are often the only documentary evidence of pre-statehood vital facts.

### Cemetery records
- Many early Vermont gravestones from the 1760s-1790s survive in town cemeteries.
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Vermont coverage.
- Sexton records are rare for this period; genealogical society transcriptions held by Vermont Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- Vermont Gazette began 1781 (Westminster). Coverage limited and concentrated in a few towns.
- Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) has some early Vermont papers.
- Legal notices (estate settlements, land disputes) are most genealogically useful for this era.

### Immigration and emigration records
- Most settlers arrived overland from southern New England — no arrival manifests.
- Town of origin sometimes in proprietors' records, church membership transfers, pension files.
- Search Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island records for where Vermont settlers came from.
- Check Quebec (BAnQ) parish registers for families near the northern Vermont border.

### Tax records
- Vermont Republic and early-state town and county tax lists; some survive from late 1770s onward.
- Held at Vermont State Archives and town vaults; some microfilmed.
- Primary substitute for census records in the 1777-1790 gap.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Name officeholders and committee members year by year.
- **Vermont Republic legislative and court records:** Vermont State Archives; petitions and court cases naming ordinary settlers.
- **Town histories (1860-1900):** Often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records; freely digitized on Google Books and Internet Archive. (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census; microfilmed church and probate records in catalog | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 federal census (indexed); some Vermont records | Subscription |
| Vermont Secretary of State — Land Records | Digitized early town land records | Free |
| Chronicling America | Some early Vermont newspapers (1780s-1790s) | Free |
| Find A Grave | Pre-statehood gravestone photos | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension and bounty land files | Subscription |
| Internet Archive / Google Books | 19th-century Vermont town histories | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic records, tax lists, militia, legislative records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) | Town histories, church records, manuscripts | In-person; some online |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | NH Grants records, Wentworth-era town charters | In-person or written inquiry |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | NY competing grants and court records for Vermont territory | In-person or written inquiry |
| Individual town clerk offices | Early land records, scattered vital records, town minutes | Contact town clerk directly |
| FamilySearch Family History Library | Microfilm of Vermont church, probate, and other records | In-person; some online via catalog |

## Records NOT online
- Town-clerk vital entries from the 1770s-1791 (individual town offices)
- Vermont Republic General Assembly and court records (Vermont State Archives)
- Town tax and assessment lists from the Vermont Republic era
- Town meeting minutes (individual town vaults)
- Church membership and disciplinary records
- New Hampshire colonial grant records (New Hampshire State Archives)
- New York competing grant and court records (New York State Archives)
- Town proprietors' minute books

## Known record losses
- No major statewide disaster affecting Vermont's pre-statehood records is documented by the tools consulted.
- Record-keeping was informal and inconsistent — many events were never created as records, not destroyed later.
- Individual town vault condition varies; ask each town clerk about early record completeness.

## Research tips
- Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — the earliest systematic resident list (~1,800 grantees). (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- The town is the key unit. Always identify the specific town, not just the county.
- No civil vital registration for this period. Default to church records first.
- Search all three land grant systems: NH Grants, NY competing grants, and Vermont Republic records.
- Use 19th-century town histories as a primary research tool. (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- The 1790 census is your anchor; work backward using tax lists and proprietors' records.
- Check Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island records for pre-migration origins.
- Search Revolutionary War pension files at NARA (Fold3) — they contain sworn family testimony.
- Check Quebec parish registers (BAnQ) for northern Vermont families.
- Vermont Republic-era tax lists substitute for the missing census in 1777-1790.

- Many early Vermont gravestones from the 1760s-1790s survive in town cemeteries.
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial Vermont coverage.
- Sexton records are rare for this period; genealogical society transcriptions held by Vermont Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- Vermont Gazette began 1781 (Westminster). Coverage limited and concentrated in a few towns.
- Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) has some early Vermont papers.
- Legal notices (estate settlements, land disputes) are most genealogically useful for this era.

### Immigration and emigration records
- Most settlers arrived overland from southern New England — no arrival manifests.
- Town of origin sometimes in proprietors' records, church membership transfers, pension files.
- Search Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island records for where Vermont settlers came from.
- Check Quebec (BAnQ) parish registers for families near the northern Vermont border.

### Tax records
- Vermont Republic and early-state town and county tax lists; some survive from late 1770s onward.
- Held at Vermont State Archives and town vaults; some microfilmed.
- Primary substitute for census records in the 1777-1790 gap.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Name officeholders and committee members year by year.
- **Vermont Republic legislative and court records:** Vermont State Archives; petitions and court cases naming ordinary settlers.
- **Town histories (1860-1900):** Often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records; freely digitized on Google Books and Internet Archive. (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census; microfilmed church and probate records in catalog | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 federal census (indexed); some Vermont records | Subscription |
| Vermont Secretary of State — Land Records | Digitized early town land records | Free |
| Chronicling America | Some early Vermont newspapers (1780s-1790s) | Free |
| Find A Grave | Pre-statehood gravestone photos | Free |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension and bounty land files | Subscription |
| Internet Archive / Google Books | 19th-century Vermont town histories | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic records, tax lists, militia, legislative records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) | Town histories, church records, manuscripts | In-person; some online |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | NH Grants records, Wentworth-era town charters | In-person or written inquiry |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | NY competing grants and court records for Vermont territory | In-person or written inquiry |
| Individual town clerk offices | Early land records, scattered vital records, town minutes | Contact town clerk directly |
| FamilySearch Family History Library | Microfilm of Vermont church, probate, and other records | In-person; some online via catalog |

## Records NOT online
- Town-clerk vital entries from the 1770s-1791 (individual town offices)
- Vermont Republic General Assembly and court records (Vermont State Archives)
- Town tax and assessment lists from the Vermont Republic era
- Town meeting minutes (individual town vaults)
- Church membership and disciplinary records
- New Hampshire colonial grant records (New Hampshire State Archives)
- New York competing grant and court records (New York State Archives)
- Town proprietors' minute books

## Known record losses
- No major statewide disaster affecting Vermont's pre-statehood records is documented by the tools consulted.
- Record-keeping was informal and inconsistent — many events were never created as records, not destroyed later.
- Individual town vault condition varies; ask each town clerk about early record completeness.

## Research tips
- Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — the earliest systematic resident list (~1,800 grantees). (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- The town is the key unit. Always identify the specific town, not just the county.
- No civil vital registration for this period. Default to church records first.
- Search all three land grant systems: NH Grants, NY competing grants, and Vermont Republic records.
- Use 19th-century town histories as a primary research tool. (FamilySearch Wiki — Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- The 1790 census is your anchor; work backward using tax lists and proprietors' records.
- Check Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island records for pre-migration origins.
- Search Revolutionary War pension files at NARA (Fold3) — they contain sworn family testimony.
- Check Quebec parish registers (BAnQ) for northern Vermont families.
- Vermont Republic-era tax lists substitute for the missing census in 1777-1790.
